- **Finite limits.** A request has 30 s in all (`ClientBuilder::timeout`, or `RequestBuilder::timeout` for one): waiting for a connection, connecting (10 s of it at most), sending, reading the response, redirects. A response body may have 16 MiB, its head 64 KiB. An unused connection is closed after 60 s.
- **Strict reading.** Bodies by `Content-Length`, chunked, or up to the end of the connection; 1xx responses are skipped. A response that could be read in two ways (two lengths, bare line feeds, folded headers, bytes after the body) is an error or keeps its connection out of the pool, so one response is never read as part of another. The code that reads a response on a connection, and decides whether the connection can carry the next request, is fuzzed every night (`response_body`): the body must end exactly where its framing says, whatever pieces the bytes arrive in, and a connection that received a byte past the body is never reused.
- **Proxies.** `ClientBuilder::proxy(Proxy::all("http://user:pass@proxy:3128")?.no_proxy(".svc.cluster.local, 10.0.0.0/8")?)`, or `Proxy::from_env()` for `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` the way curl reads them (never read unless asked). It returns `Result<Option<Proxy>, Error>`, `None` when the environment names no proxy: `if let Some(proxy) = Proxy::from_env()? { builder = builder.proxy(proxy); }`. `https` goes through a `CONNECT` tunnel, so the proxy sees only the host name; the credentials go to the proxy, never to the server. Plain `http://` proxies only, for now (no SOCKS, no TLS to the proxy itself).
- **Compression.** Responses are asked for with `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate` and decompressed as they arrive (`ClientBuilder::decompress(false)` turns it off; a request with its own `Accept-Encoding` gets the bytes as sent). The size limit applies to the decompressed body, so 32 KiB that would expand to gigabytes fails at the limit instead of filling memory; the gzip checksum is checked, and a body cut short is an error, not a shorter body.
- **Streaming.** `RequestBuilder::send_streaming()` returns once the head has arrived; `StreamingResponse::chunk()` gives the body piece by piece (64 KiB at most, decompressed), with no limit on its size and the timeout applying to each piece. Read to its end, the connection goes back to the pool; dropped before, it is closed (over HTTP/2, only its stream is reset).
- **Errors that say what to do.** `Error::kind` is one of `Request`, `Connect`, `Timeout`, `TooLarge`, `Redirect`, `Closed`, `Protocol`, `Status`, `Decode` and `Proxy`, each with a giong code (GIONG-E1101 to E1110) and a page in [docs/errors](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md); `Error::is_transient` says whether retrying can help. Any status is a `Response`; `error_for_status` turns 4xx and 5xx into an error with the start of the body.

The client is not `Send`, like everything in giong: make one per worker (in the closure given to `Runtime::run`) and clone it into that worker's tasks.

### Client performance

Measured with `bench/http-client.sh` against reqwest 0.12 (rustls, HTTP/2 on, on a current-thread Tokio runtime). Each client runs on one core and shares one client between 64 tasks that send `GET` requests back to back and read every body; giong-http's server answers on the other three cores of a 4-vCPU virtual machine (Xeon 2.3 GHz, Linux 6.18), over TCP on 127.0.0.1. `json` is a 27-byte answer, `users` an 8.5 KiB one. Medians of 5 rounds of 5 s, with the range in brackets; requests per second.

Over HTTP/1.1 (both clients told to speak it, since the server also offers HTTP/2):

| Client | Connections | `json` | `users` | `json` over HTTPS | `users` over HTTPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **giong-http** | 64 | **150.1k** (120–167k) | **91.7k** (88–136k) | **145.3k** (118–156k) | **81.2k** (76–93k) |
| giong-http, its default | 16 | 113.8k (84–126k) | 82.3k (78–100k) | 99.9k (80–110k) | 84.2k (65–90k) |
| reqwest, its default | 64 (one per task) | 84.7k (66–87k) | 58.1k (56–81k) | 84.6k (62–88k) | 48.8k (40–56k) |

Over HTTP/2, every request on one connection:

| Client | `json` over HTTPS | `users` over HTTPS | `json`, prior knowledge | `users`, prior knowledge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **giong-http** | **250.7k** (242–264k) | **64.2k** (55–66k) | **265.7k** (251–273k) | **68.4k** (68–71k) |
| reqwest | 122.9k (116–135k) | 48.3k (43–51k) | 123.1k (119–124k) | 56.0k (43–65k) |

- **HTTP/1.1 with as many connections: 1.6 to 1.8 times reqwest's requests per second, with a lower p99** (0.66–1.5 ms against 1.15–2.0 ms). Every client's core is the limit (99–100% busy); the server's three cores are not (50–159% of 300).
- **With its default of 16 connections, still 1.2 to 1.7 times reqwest with 64.** Fewer requests in flight means fewer of them handled per trip into the kernel; the default is there to spare the server, and `max_connections_per_host` raises it.
- **HTTP/2: 2.0 to 2.2 times reqwest on small answers, 1.2 to 1.3 times on 8.5 KiB ones**, with half the latency on small ones (p50 0.24 against 0.49 ms, p99 0.41 against 0.84 ms over HTTPS). On one connection the two ends take turns (the client writes every request queued at once, the server answers them all at once), so neither is busy all the time: giong-http's core is 51–63% busy, reqwest's 60–88%. With 8.5 KiB answers the server's single worker for the single connection is the limit (94% of a core), which is why HTTP/1.1 over 64 connections, spread over the server's three workers, gets more there; with small answers, HTTP/2 gets 1.7 times what HTTP/1.1 does.
- Not measured: a server on another machine, `POST` bodies, more than one client core, many hosts at once.

Results are in `bench/results/http-client/`.

## Not there yet

Server push. Routing and compression of responses are in [`giong-web`](https://giong.run/docs/giong-web.md). In the client: cookies, `br` and `zstd`, SOCKS proxies, HTTP/2 through an `http://` proxy (HTTPS through a proxy's tunnel gets HTTP/2), the `Upgrade: h2c` handshake.

## Tests

`cargo test -p giong-http --all-features`: 66 unit tests (including 500,000 random inputs for the parser and the chunked decoder, 300,000 for the client's response parser and URLs, 100,000 responses read by the client on a connection in random pieces, 50,000 damaged gzip and deflate bodies, 200,000 HPACK header blocks and Huffman strings, 3,000 HTTP/2 connections whose every frame is checked, and 3,000 from the client's side, checking what it holds and writes), 44 HTTP/2 tests (22 end-to-end on real sockets with a client that writes its frames by hand, 22 of frames, HPACK, requests and stream memory), 30 end-to-end tests of the server on real sockets (one of them over a Unix socket, four of the memory budget for requests being received, one of them with bodies received straight into the request buffer, one of bodies from 64 KiB to 3 MiB received straight into the request buffer between other requests), 14 end-to-end tests of streamed bodies (a 250 KB upload read piece by piece with the connection used again after it, chunked uploads, bodies past the handler's limit, broken framing, nothing read and no `100 Continue` until the handler asks, a handler that answers early, a body cut short, the timeout of each piece; streamed responses chunked and sent piece by piece, to an HTTP/1.0 client, without a body for `HEAD`, 204 and 304, aborted, and stopped when the client goes away), 12 end-to-end HTTPS tests with a rustls client (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, pipelining, a 3 MB body, 400/413 errors, idle connections, clients that do not speak TLS, graceful shutdown, 16 client threads at once), 22 end-to-end tests of the client against this server, against servers that misbehave on purpose and through proxies, 15 of the client over HTTP/2 (against this server through ALPN, over kernel TLS where the kernel has it, and with prior knowledge, and against servers that refuse streams, send GOAWAY, reset streams, send malformed responses, close early, send past the window or wait for a window the client grants only once the connection has gone quiet), 15 documentation examples. One more client test, ignored by default (`-- --ignored`), fetches from crates.io over HTTPS.

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/giong-grpc/README.md -->

# giong-grpc

gRPC for the [giong](https://giong.run/docs/giong.md) runtime: servers and clients over [giong-http](https://giong.run/docs/giong-http.md)'s HTTP/2, with messages read as [giong-proto](https://giong.run/docs/giong-proto.md) views that borrow from the bytes received. Nothing from the Tokio ecosystem, and no `protoc` to install: [giong-grpc-build](https://giong.run/docs/giong-grpc-build.md) parses the `.proto` files in Rust.

It interoperates with grpc-go in both directions on the test cases of [gRPC's interoperability specification](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/interop-test-descriptions.md), on io_uring and on epoll, in CI ([`interop/run.sh`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/giong-grpc/interop/run.sh)).

> **New in giong 1.1.**

```toml
[dependencies]
giong = "1"
giong-http = "1"
giong-grpc = "1"
giong-proto = "1"

[build-dependencies]
giong-grpc-build = "1"
```

`build.rs`:

```rust,ignore
fn main() {
    giong_grpc_build::compile(&["proto/greeter.proto"], &["proto"]).unwrap();
}
```

`proto/greeter.proto`:

```proto
syntax = "proto3";
package hello.v1;

service Greeter {
  rpc SayHello(HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);
  rpc SayHelloMany(HelloRequest) returns (stream HelloReply);
}

message HelloRequest { string name = 1; uint32 count = 2; }
message HelloReply { string message = 1; }
```

The server implements the trait generated for the service, one method for each rpc:

```rust,ignore
mod pb {
    include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/giong_proto.rs"));
}
use giong_grpc::{Code, Reply, Request, Server, Sink, Status};
use pb::hello::v1::greeter::{Greeter, GreeterServer};
use pb::hello::v1::{HelloReply, HelloRequest};

struct Hello;

impl Greeter for Hello {
    async fn say_hello(
        &self,
        request: Request<HelloRequest<'static>>,
    ) -> Result<Reply<HelloReply<'static>>, Status> {
        // A view over the bytes received: `name()` borrows from them.
        let name = request.message()?.name();
        if name.is_empty() {
            return Err(Status::new(Code::InvalidArgument, "name must not be empty"));
        }
        Reply::new(&HelloReply { message: &format!("Xin chào, {name}!"), ..Default::default() })
    }

    async fn say_hello_many(
        &self,
        request: Request<HelloRequest<'static>>,
        mut responses: Sink<HelloReply<'static>>,
    ) -> Result<(), Status> {
        let message = request.message()?;
        for n in 1..=message.count() {
            let text = format!("Xin chào, {} ({n})!", message.name());
            // Waits while the client is slow to read; fails once it is gone.
            responses.send(&HelloReply { message: &text, ..Default::default() }).await?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    // One server per worker thread, all on the same port.
    giong::Builder::new().build()?.run(|_worker| async {
        let listener = giong::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:50051").expect("bind");
        let grpc = Server::new().add(GreeterServer::new(Hello));
        giong_http::Server::new().serve(listener, grpc).await;
    })
}
```

The client calls through the generated `GreeterClient`:

```rust,ignore
use giong_grpc::{CallOptions, Channel};
use pb::hello::v1::greeter::GreeterClient;

let greeter = GreeterClient::new(Channel::new("http://127.0.0.1:50051")?);
let request = HelloRequest { name: "An", count: 3, ..Default::default() };

let reply = greeter.say_hello(&request, CallOptions::new()).await?;
println!("{}", reply.message()?.message());

let mut replies = greeter.say_hello_many(&request, CallOptions::new()).await?;
while let Some(received) = replies.message().await? {
    println!("{}", received.message()?.message());
}
```

[`examples/grpc-hello`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/examples/grpc-hello) is this program, complete, with health and reflection.

## What it does

- **The four kinds of method**: unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional, with requests and responses flowing at the same time on one HTTP/2 stream.
- **Messages without copies.** A message is decoded as a view over the bytes that arrived: it is not copied out of the piece of the stream it came in, and messages that arrived together share that piece. Responses are encoded from structs whose fields borrow.
- **Deadlines on both sides.** A client sends its timeout and enforces it; a server enforces the one it was sent, or its own default. A call past its deadline ends with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` and its handler is dropped.
- **Cancellation that reaches the handler.** When a client cancels, drops its stream or disappears, the handler's future is dropped at its next `.await`, and `Sink::send` and `RequestStream::message` fail in a handler that is still running.
- **Backpressure.** Sending waits for the reader, so a slow reader slows its writer down and nothing queues without bound.
- **Streams that batch themselves.** The messages a handler sends before it next waits leave in one write (up to 16 KiB at a time); nothing is held back for more to come, and there is no flush to call.
- **Metadata**, text and binary (`-bin`), before and after the messages; statuses with details.
- **gzip**, per message, off by default.
- **TLS** through `giong_http::Server::serve_tls` and `https://` addresses (ALPN), with private authorities and client certificates.
- **Health checking** (`grpc.health.v1.Health`: Check, List, Watch) and **server reflection** (`v1` and `v1alpha`): `grpcurl list`, `describe` and calls work without the `.proto` files.
- **Errors with codes.** The statuses giong-grpc raises itself carry `GIONG-E4101` to `GIONG-E4110`, with what happened and how to fix it in the message ([docs/errors](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/README.md#giong-grpc)).

## The four kinds of method

| In the `.proto` | The handler takes | and returns | The client method returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rpc M(Req) returns (Resp)` | `Request<Req>` | `Reply<Resp>` | `Reply<Resp>` |
| `rpc M(Req) returns (stream Resp)` | `Request<Req>`, `Sink<Resp>` | `()` | `ResponseStream<Resp>` |
| `rpc M(stream Req) returns (Resp)` | `RequestStream<Req>` | `Reply<Resp>` | `ClientStreaming<Req, Resp>` |
| `rpc M(stream Req) returns (stream Resp)` | `RequestStream<Req>`, `Sink<Resp>` | `()` | (`RequestSink<Req>`, `ResponseStream<Resp>`) |

Every handler returns `Result<_, Status>`. An `Err` ends the call with that status, and the client gets it as the `Err` of its call.

A bidirectional call:

```rust,ignore
let (mut requests, mut responses) = chat.converse(CallOptions::new());
requests.send(&Line { text: "hello", ..Default::default() }).await?;
while let Some(received) = responses.message().await? {
    let line = received.message()?;
    if line.text() == "bye" {
        break;
    }
    requests.send(&Line { text: "and then?", ..Default::default() }).await?;
}
requests.finish(); // the server sees the end of the requests
```

## Limits

Every limit is finite by default.

| What | Default | Set with |
|---|---|---|
| One message, compressed or once decompressed | 4 MiB | `Server::max_message_size`, `ChannelBuilder::max_message_size` |
| A call, on the client | 30 s | `CallOptions::timeout`, `ChannelBuilder::timeout` |
| A call whose client sent no deadline, on the server | 1 h | `Server::default_timeout` |
| Opening a connection | 10 s | `ChannelBuilder::connect_timeout` |
| Connections, concurrent streams, header sizes, a client's silence between two messages | giong-http's | `giong_http::Server` |

## Health and reflection

```rust,ignore
use giong_grpc::health::Health;
use giong_grpc::reflection::Reflection;

// Both are Send and Sync: made once, shared by the servers of every worker.
let health = Health::new();
health.set("hello.v1.Greeter", true);
let reflection = Reflection::new(&[pb::FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET, giong_grpc::health::FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET])?;

let grpc = Server::new()
    .add(GreeterServer::new(Hello))
    .add(health.service())
    .add(reflection.v1())
    .add(reflection.v1alpha());
```

```text
$ grpcurl -plaintext localhost:50051 list
grpc.health.v1.Health
grpc.reflection.v1.ServerReflection
grpc.reflection.v1alpha.ServerReflection
hello.v1.Greeter
$ grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"name": "An"}' localhost:50051 hello.v1.Greeter/SayHello
{
  "message": "Xin chào, An!"
}
```

`health.set(service, false)` from any thread tells load balancers to stop sending calls; `health.set_all_not_serving()` does it for every service at the start of a shutdown. Reflection tells anyone who can reach the port what the server's API is: leave it off a server whose API is not public.

## Measured against tonic

`bench/grpc.sh`, against tonic 0.14 (prost, hyper, Tokio) with the same service: unary calls with 100-byte and 10,000-byte payloads, round trips on a bidirectional stream, and server streams of 1,000 messages of 100 bytes. A 4-core cloud VM (Xeon 2.1 GHz, Linux 6.18, io_uring), the median of 10 rounds of 5 s; the method is at the top of the script and the raw data in [`bench/results/grpc/`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/bench/results/grpc).

One server thread, loaded from three other cores until its core is the limit, with tonic's client and with giong-grpc's as the load generator:

| Workload | Load | tonic | giong-grpc | | Server CPU per call or message, tonic → giong-grpc |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| unary, 100 B | tonic | 172,842 calls/s | 259,030 | +50% | 5.54 → 3.62 µs |
| unary, 100 B | giong | 174,525 | 227,408 | +30% | 5.46 → 4.14 µs |
| unary, 10 kB | tonic | 71,918 | 89,862 | +25% | 13.25 → 10.44 µs |
| unary, 10 kB | giong | 75,010 | 90,463 | +21% | 12.77 → 10.51 µs |
| bidirectional round trips | tonic | 550,596 msg/s | 813,260 | +48% | 1.74 → 1.18 µs |
| bidirectional round trips | giong | 542,390 | 816,094 | +50% | 1.76 → 1.17 µs |
| server stream | tonic | 2,917,860 msg/s | 11,694,153 | 4.0× | 0.329 → 0.081 µs |
| server stream | giong | 2,985,038 | 11,394,657 | 3.8× | 0.321 → 0.084 µs |

No workload is behind on the server side. 10,000-byte unary calls from tonic's client were 7.5% behind until giong-http's HTTP/2 server sent the answers to a burst of short requests in one write: it cut its output at 64 KiB, and with one write in flight per connection each further write waited a turn of the worker. With 64 calls in flight per connection (`TASKS=128`, [`tasks-128/`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/bench/results/grpc/tasks-128)) giong-grpc's server does 78,401 calls/s against tonic's 70,778 (+10.8%) under tonic's client and 103,618 against 70,002 (+48%) under its own. The server stream is ahead by that much because the messages a handler sends in a row leave in one write.

One client thread, against a server with three threads (tonic's, then giong-grpc's):

| Workload | Server | tonic client | giong-grpc client | |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| unary, 100 B | tonic | 87,301 calls/s | 94,606 | +8% |
| unary, 100 B | giong | 137,046 | 143,424 | +5% |
| unary, 10 kB | tonic | 51,879 | 58,964 | +14% |
| unary, 10 kB | giong | 57,778 | 60,384 | +5% |
| bidirectional round trips | tonic | 253,018 msg/s | 248,773 | **−1.7%** |
| bidirectional round trips | giong | 489,518 | 498,710 | +2% |
| server stream | tonic | 5,627,548 msg/s | 5,698,860 | +1% |
| server stream | giong | 9,399,474 | 9,446,808 | +1% |

Round trips against tonic's server are level (−1.7%; +0.8% to +2.2% in earlier runs): both clients used about three quarters of their core, so that row measures the server. Server streams from giong-grpc's server were 10% to 18% behind until two things changed: `ResponseStream::message` returns a message that has already arrived without setting up the future that waits for more (it was rebuilt for every message), and a received HTTP/2 frame is handed to the reader as it is instead of being joined to the next ones. The giong-grpc server in the client runs listens with `TcpListener::bind_balanced`, so that the client's two connections always land on two of its three workers: with the kernel's choice they sometimes shared one, and that row moved by a third between rounds. Not measured: client streams of many messages in a row, where the giong-grpc client still hands the connection one message at a time.

Memory: with 1,000 bidirectional streams open on 10 connections, the server's resident memory grew by 5.7 kB a stream with giong-grpc and 11.6 kB with tonic.

The giong-http server in these runs has `max_body_size(4 << 20)`: the HTTP/2 window a stream starts with is a share of the server's body budget (half of it divided by `max_concurrent_streams`, 5 KiB with the defaults), and a request larger than that window waits for a WINDOW_UPDATE. A service whose requests are larger than 5 KiB should set `max_body_size` to its message limit, which makes the first window 20 KiB for 4 MiB.

## Not there

Client-side load balancing and name resolution beyond DNS, retries and hedging (a failed call is returned, not sent again), gRPC-Web, compression other than gzip, and the `google.rpc.Status` details message (its bytes are available: `Status::details`).

## Tests

```sh
cargo test -p giong-grpc                 # calls, faults, health, reflection, generated code
giong-grpc/interop/run.sh                # grpc-go both directions, grpcurl (needs Go)
GIONG_SOAK_SECS=3600 cargo test --release -p giong-grpc --test soak -- --ignored --nocapture
(cd giong-grpc && cargo +nightly fuzz run framing)   # also: gzip timeout status_message metadata descriptors
```

The soak runs calls of every kind with faults mixed in (cancels, dropped streams, deadlines, connections cut in the middle of a message, bytes that are not HTTP/2) and then checks that no handler, descriptor, driver operation or memory was left behind.

The minimum Rust version is 1.80, as for giong.

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/giong-postgres/README.md -->

# giong-postgres

A PostgreSQL client and connection pool for the [giong](https://giong.run/docs/giong.md) runtime. It speaks the wire protocol itself (no libpq), encrypts with [`giong-tls`](https://giong.run/docs/giong-tls.md), and depends on nothing from the Tokio ecosystem.

```toml
[dependencies]
giong = "1.5.1"
giong-postgres = "1.5.1"
```

```rust,no_run
use giong_postgres::{Client, Config};

fn main() -> Result<(), giong_postgres::Error> {
    let config = Config::from_url("postgres://app:secret@localhost/shop")?;
    giong::block_on(async {
        let client = Client::connect(&config).await?;
        let rows = client
            .query("SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE price < $1", &[&100i32])
            .await?;
        for row in &rows {
            let id: i64 = row.get("id")?;
            let name: &str = row.get("name")?;
            println!("{id} {name}");
        }
        Ok(())
    })
}
```

In a service, make one `Pool` per worker. Nothing is shared between threads, so nothing is locked:

```rust,no_run
use giong_postgres::{Config, Pool};

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let config = Config::from_url("postgres://app:secret@db.internal/shop")?;
    giong::Builder::new().build()?.run(move |_worker| {
        let pool = Pool::new(config.clone(), 4);
        async move {
            // ... serve requests, each one calling pool.query(..) ...
            let row = pool.query_one("SELECT count(*) FROM orders", &[]).await.unwrap();
            let n: i64 = row.get(0).unwrap();
            println!("{n} orders");
        }
    })
}
```

## What it does

- **Pipelining across tasks.** Tasks that share a connection send their statements together, and one round trip answers all of them. A few connections serve hundreds of concurrent tasks without each task waiting for a connection of its own.
- **Prepared statements, kept.** Every statement is prepared the first time a connection runs it and kept in a bounded cache (256 per connection by default), so from then on it takes one round trip. When the schema changes under a cached statement (`ALTER TABLE`, a view replaced), the statement is prepared again and run once more, so the caller sees no error; inside a transaction the server has already aborted the transaction, so that one call fails with the server's error and the next one is prepared again. Stale statements are recognised by SQLSTATE and the server's routine name, so this works whatever language the server writes its messages in.
- **Binary results for the common types** (`boolean`, `bytea`, the integers, `oid`, the floats, `timestamptz`), and text for the rest. A column of a text-format type (`uuid`, `numeric`, `date`, `timestamp`, `jsonb`, arrays, `interval`, `inet` and the like) can be read as a `String`; a binary one is read as its Rust type in the [table](#types) below, or cast in SQL (`created_at::text`).
- **A pool per worker.** Statements that stand alone share connections; `pool.get()` takes one connection for a transaction, session settings or a slow statement. When it comes back, a transaction left open is rolled back and the session is reset (settings, temporary tables, advisory locks, `LISTEN`, cursors), so nothing one task did reaches the next. Tasks waiting in `get()` are served in the order they came, even while shared statements keep every connection busy. `get()` can take every connection of the pool: while all of them are held, the pool's own `query` waits too, and fails with `GIONG-E3009` when the wait runs out, so size a pool for the transactions that run at once and one connection more. Transactions and session changes never run on the shared connections: the pool's own methods refuse `BEGIN`, `SET`, `LISTEN`, `PREPARE`, temporary tables and the like before sending them, and a batch that leaves a transaction open closes its connection rather than let the statements of other tasks run inside it. The pool steers new statements away from a connection whose oldest statement has been running for more than 5 ms, so a slow query does not hold up the fast ones behind it. Connections are closed after 10 minutes unused and replaced after 30 minutes, or as soon as their server turns out to be a standby after a failover.
- **TLS on by default for remote hosts, always verified.** SCRAM-SHA-256, MD5, and clear-text passwords only over TLS or to this machine. `require_auth` limits the methods the server may ask for. SCRAM's key derivation runs on a thread of its own, once per password and salt, so connecting does not stall the other tasks of the worker.
- **Errors that say what to do.** Every error has an `ErrorKind`; errors from the server carry the SQLSTATE code and every field the server sent (`detail`, `hint`, `constraint`...).
- **Finite limits everywhere.** Connecting, running a statement, the size of a result, the statement cache and waiting for the pool all have a limit by default, so nothing waits forever and nothing grows without bound.

## Connecting

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use giong_postgres::{Config, Error};

fn configs() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let config = Config::from_url("postgres://app:secret@db.internal:5432/shop?sslmode=verify-full")?;

    let same_place = Config::new()
        .host("db.internal")
        .user("app")
        .password("secret")
        .database("shop")
        .statement_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5));
    let _ = (config, same_place);
    Ok(())
}
```

A URL is `postgres://user:password@host:port/dbname?param=value` (`postgresql://` too). The host can be an IPv6 address in brackets, or, as with libpq, empty with the socket directory in a `host` parameter: `postgres:///shop?host=/var/run/postgresql`. The parameters understood are `sslmode`, `sslrootcert`, `host`, `port`, `user`, `password`, `dbname`, `application_name`, `connect_timeout` (seconds) and `require_auth`. Any other parameter is an error, not silently ignored.

**TLS.** Unless `Config::tls` or `sslmode` says otherwise:

| Where the server is | What happens |
|---|---|
| A Unix socket (a host starting with `/`) | No TLS. |
| A loopback address (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`) | No TLS. |
| Anywhere else | TLS, with the certificate checked against the certificate authorities installed on the machine and against the host name. |

`sslmode=disable` turns TLS off. `require`, `verify-ca` and `verify-full` all check the certificate and the host name, which is stricter than libpq (libpq checks nothing for `require`). `prefer` and `allow` are refused, because they fall back to an unencrypted connection without saying so. `sslrootcert=/path/ca.pem` trusts only that authority; in code, use `Tls::Verify(TlsConnector::with_root_pem(..)?)`. When TLS is requested and the server does not support it, connecting fails.

A clear-text password is never sent over an unencrypted connection to another machine: the connection fails with `ErrorKind::Auth` instead.

**Authentication.** Without TLS (a Unix socket, a loopback address, `sslmode=disable`), nothing proves the server is the real one, and an impostor could ask for MD5 instead of SCRAM or let the client in without asking. `Config::require_auth(&[AuthMethod::ScramSha256])`, or `require_auth=scram-sha-256` in the URL (libpq's names, comma-separated, without libpq's `!` negations), refuses any other method before anything is sent for the password.

### Behind PgBouncer

In transaction mode, PgBouncer gives each transaction any server connection, so two things need setting up:

- **Prepared statements** need PgBouncer 1.21 or later with `max_prepared_statements` above 0 (it then prepares them on whichever server connection runs them). With it, the statement cache works as usual. Without it, prepared statements cannot work through PgBouncer in transaction mode, whatever `statement_cache_capacity` is.
- **The statement timeout** cannot be sent when connecting: PgBouncer refuses the connection, and neither `track_extra_parameters` nor `ignore_startup_parameters` passes it on to the server (checked with PgBouncer 1.22). Call `Config::statement_timeout(None)` and set the limit on the role: `ALTER ROLE app SET statement_timeout = '30s'`. Connecting without `None` fails with an error that says this.

Both are tested in CI against PgBouncer in transaction mode.

## API

| | |
|---|---|
| `Client::connect(&config)` | Opens a connection: TCP or Unix socket, TLS, authentication, all within `connect_timeout`. |
| `client.query(sql, &[&a, &b])` | All the rows, as `Vec<Row>`. Parameters are `$1`, `$2`... |
| `client.query_one(..)`, `query_opt(..)` | Exactly one row (`ErrorKind::RowCount` otherwise); at most one. |
| `client.execute(..)` | The number of rows affected. |
| `client.batch_execute(sql)` | Several statements separated by `;`, through the simple protocol, with no parameters and no results. For migrations and setup. |
| `client.transaction()` | Starts a transaction and borrows the client mutably until it ends. `tx.commit()` or `tx.rollback()`; dropping the transaction rolls it back. A `COMMIT` that the server turned into a rollback (because of an earlier error) is an error, not a success. |
| `client.cancel_token()` | A `CancelToken` whose `cancel()` asks the server, over a separate connection, to stop the statement running now. A token taken from a `PooledClient` stops working when the connection goes back to the pool, and a connection that goes back while such a request is on its way is closed rather than lent again, so it cannot cancel another task's statement. |
| `client.parameter(name)` | A setting the server reported, such as `server_version` or `TimeZone`. |
| `client.is_closed()`, `client.in_flight()` | Whether the connection is closed; how many requests are waiting for their answer. |
| `row.get::<T>(column)` | A column by position or name, converted to `T` (see [Types](#types)). Borrowed types (`&str`, `&[u8]`) borrow from the row. |
| `row.is_null(column)`, `row.columns()`, `row.len()` | Whether a value is `NULL`; the columns' names and types; how many there are. |
| `Pool::new(config, max_size)` | A pool for the current worker. Connections are opened when needed, up to `max_size`. Size it to the database server's cores, shared among the workers (see [Performance](#performance)). |
| `.wait_timeout(duration)` | How long `get()` and the statement methods wait when every connection is taken, 5 s by default. |
| `.idle_timeout(duration)`, `.max_lifetime(duration)` | Close a connection unused for this long (10 min by default); replace one older than this (30 min, less up to 10% so that connections opened together are not replaced together). |
| `pool.query(..)` and the other statement methods | Run on the least busy connection, pipelined with other tasks' statements. They refuse transaction statements, session changes and `COPY ... FROM STDIN` before sending them (`ErrorKind::Statement`). |
| `Config::batch_reads(true)` | Lets the pool send the `SELECT`s waiting for one shared connection under one `Sync`, up to 16, never waiting for more (see [Batched reads](#batched-reads)). Off by default. |
| `pool.get()` | A `PooledClient` for this task alone, which derefs to `Client`. For transactions, session settings and statements known to be slow. Served in the order asked. When it is dropped, a transaction left open is rolled back and, if anything was sent, the session is reset; settings given to `Config` survive the reset. |
| `pool.stats()` | Connections open, taken, being opened; requests in flight; tasks waiting; and counters for connections opened, connect errors, wait timeouts and connections recycled. |
| `Config::require_auth(&[AuthMethod::..])` | The only authentication methods the server may ask for. |

A `Client` belongs to the worker that opened it (it is not `Send`, like everything in giong). Its methods take `&self`, so tasks share one by cloning an `Rc` or by holding a reference, and their statements are pipelined.

## Types

| Rust | PostgreSQL |
|---|---|
| `bool` | `boolean` |
| `i16`, `i32`, `i64` | `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint` (any of them, checked for range); `oid` |
| `f32`, `f64` | `real`, `double precision` |
| `&str`, `String` | `text`, `varchar`, `char(n)`, `name`; as parameters, any type the server can parse from text (`uuid`, `numeric`, `date`, `json`...); as results, any column the rest of this table does not list |
| `&[u8]`, `Vec<u8>` | `bytea` |
| `SystemTime` | `timestamptz` |
| `Option<T>` | `NULL` or a value |

Integers convert between the three integer types when the value fits and fail when it does not, with an error that names the parameter or column, so a conversion never loses anything silently. Implement `ToSql` and `FromSql` for your own types.

## Errors

`Error` is cheap to clone, implements `std::error::Error`, and converts into `io::Error`. `error.kind()` says what went wrong. Each kind has a giong error code, shown in front of the message and linked to its page in [docs/errors](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md) (`GIONG-E3003: password authentication failed for user "app". See …`); after `?` into an `io::Error`, `giong::error::code(&err)` finds it:

| `ErrorKind` | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Config` | [E3001](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3001.md) | The configuration or URL is not valid. |
| `Connect` | [E3002](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3002.md) | Name resolution, TCP, TLS, or the connect timeout. Also an unknown database (`3D000`). |
| `Auth` | [E3003](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3003.md) | The server refused the credentials, or asked for a method this crate does not support. |
| `Db` | [E3004](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3004.md) | The server reported an error for the statement; `error.server_code()` is the SQLSTATE (`23505` for a unique violation...) and `error.db()` has every field. A `COMMIT` that the server turned into a rollback is `Db` with code `25P02` and no `db()`. |
| `Type` | [E3005](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3005.md) | A value could not be converted between Rust and PostgreSQL. The message names the parameter or column and suggests the Rust type to use. |
| `RowCount` | [E3006](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3006.md) | `query_one` found no row, or more than one. |
| `TooLarge` | [E3007](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3007.md) | The result was larger than `max_result_size`. The connection stays usable. |
| `Closed` | [E3008](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3008.md) | The connection is closed. A `Pool` replaces it by itself. Also a cancel token whose pooled connection went back to the pool. |
| `PoolTimeout` | [E3009](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3009.md) | No pooled connection became free within `wait_timeout`. |
| `Protocol` | [E3010](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3010.md) | The server sent something this crate cannot understand. The connection is closed. |
| `Statement` | [E3011](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3011.md) | Refused before sending, on the connections a `Pool` shares: a transaction statement, a statement that changes the session (`SET`, `LISTEN`, `PREPARE`, temporary tables...), or `COPY ... FROM STDIN`. Use `pool.get()`. The check reads the statement, not what a function does: `SELECT set_config('search_path', 'x', false)` is sent, and changes the session for every task that shares the connection. |

`error.is_transient()` is true for errors worth retrying after a pause: connecting, a closed connection, a pool wait timeout, and the server's serialization failure (`40001`), deadlock (`40P01`), lock not available (`55P03`), too many connections (`53300`), connection errors (class `08`), shutdown or startup (`57P01`, `57P02`, `57P03`) and standby (`25006`). Retry a whole transaction, not its failed statement.

An error from the server affects only its own statement: the statements that other tasks pipelined on the same connection get their own results. Two things close the connection instead, and every statement sent on it after them fails with `ErrorKind::Closed`: `COPY ... FROM STDIN` on a `Client` (COPY is not supported yet; the pool refuses it), and a `batch_execute` that leaves a transaction open on a pool's shared connection.

## Limits

| Setting | Default | What happens at the limit |
|---|---|---|
| `Config::connect_timeout` | 10 s | `ErrorKind::Connect`, "connect timeout". |
| `Config::statement_timeout` | 30 s | Sent as the session's `statement_timeout`, so the server cancels exactly the statement that ran too long (SQLSTATE `57014`). From 1 ms to `i32::MAX` ms (24.8 days); outside that, connecting fails with `ErrorKind::Config`. `None` sends nothing and leaves the limit to the server or the role. |
| `Config::max_result_size` | 64 MiB of row data | `ErrorKind::TooLarge`; the rest of the result is read and thrown away. A notice larger than this is skipped; an error message larger than this fails its statement with `TooLarge`. Either way the connection stays usable. |
| `Config::statement_cache_capacity` | 256 per connection | The least recently used statement is closed. 0 prepares and closes every statement each time. |
| `Pool::wait_timeout` | 5 s | `ErrorKind::PoolTimeout`. It bounds the wait for a connection; a task that opens a new connection itself waits up to `connect_timeout` instead. |
| `Pool::idle_timeout` | 10 min | The connection is closed. |
| `Pool::max_lifetime` | 30 min, less up to 10% | The connection is closed once no statement uses it, and a new one is opened when needed. |
| Statements on one pooled connection at a time | 1024 | The statement methods use another connection, or wait for room. A `Client` used directly has no such bound: its callers decide how many tasks share it. |

## Performance

Measured with `bench/postgres.sh` against tokio-postgres 0.7.18 with deadpool-postgres 0.14.2 (Tokio 1.54, current-thread runtime). Each client runs on one core; the same PostgreSQL 16 server runs on the other three cores of a 4-vCPU virtual machine (Xeon 2.1 GHz, Linux 6.18), reached over TCP on 127.0.0.1. 64 tasks issue statements back to back: `point` reads one row by primary key, `list` reads 100 rows, and every column of every row is decoded (`i64`, two `&str`, `SystemTime`). The figures are medians of 5 rounds of 5 s (3 rounds for the other pool sizes), with the range in brackets.

A pool, on one client core:

| Client | Connections | `point` statements/s | p99 | `list` statements/s | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **giong-postgres** | 3 | **311.4k** (308–322k) | **0.43 ms** | **71.3k** (70–74k) | **2.0 ms** |
| giong-postgres | 4 | 303.8k (277–317k) | 2.9 ms | 72.9k (64–76k) | 4.9 ms |
| tokio-postgres + deadpool | 4 | 55.4k (53–56k) | 1.7 ms | 25.4k (24–26k) | 3.9 ms |
| tokio-postgres + deadpool | 64, its best | 93.8k (91–97k) | 1.5 ms | 28.6k (27–29k) | 4.1 ms |

- **Against deadpool at its best: 3.3× the point lookups and 2.5× the 100-row reads, at a third to a half of the p99.** deadpool's client core is the limit (98–99% busy): every statement is a pool checkout, a round trip and a wake-up. giong-postgres sends the statements of all 64 tasks in a few writes and reads their answers in a few reads.
- **Size the pool to the database's cores.** With more connections than the server has cores (4 on 3 here), one backend at a time waits for a core, and the statements pipelined on its connection, about 16 of them, wait with it: the same throughput, but a p99 of 2.9 ms instead of 0.43. 8 connections give 253.8k at a p99 of 1.4 ms (8.6 ms for 100 rows); 2 connections leave a server core idle, 183.9k. With several workers, the connections of all their pools add up. Statements that wait on disk or on locks need more connections than this.
- **One connection shared by every task** (both libraries pipeline): the single backend process is the limit, one server core at 100%, and here giong-postgres is behind: its medians are 7–9% lower (point 47.7k against 51.4k, list 18.7k against 20.5k; the same with the two run in the other order), though the ranges of the rounds overlap, and it uses less of its core (50% against 52%, 43% against 64%). Both send the same messages, one `Sync` per statement, and the server spends half of its time in `send()`, writing one reply per statement and waking the client for it, and the gap is in that part (a quarter of the server's time with giong-postgres, against slightly less with tokio-postgres, whose busier client needs waking less often). Sending several statements under one `Sync` cuts the server's work, but it runs them in one transaction, so it is only done by a pool with `batch_reads` (below). Use a `Pool`, where the client is the limit and giong-postgres does 5.5 times as much.

### Batched reads

With `Config::batch_reads(true)`, the `SELECT`s that a pool's shared connection has waiting when it writes go to the server under one `Sync`, at most 16, behind a prepared statement that makes their transaction read-only; a statement never waits for others to join it. The server then sends one reply and wakes the client once per batch rather than once per statement, which matters when the server is the busy side. Measured with `bench/postgres.sh` (`batch` mode, 3 rounds of 5 s, 64 tasks, `point`; results in `bench/results/postgres/batch/`):

| Server cores | Connections | without batches | p99 | with batches | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 58.7k (54–61k) | 2.0 ms | **198.3k** (197–204k) | **0.56 ms** |
| 1 | 4 | 50.5k (49–55k) | 12.5 ms | **171.9k** (167–187k) | **0.75 ms** |
| 3 | 4 | 314.2k (273–327k) | 2.5 ms | **370.4k** (318–372k) | **0.39 ms** |

- **3.4 times the point lookups when the database is the limit, and up to 18% more with it on three cores**, where the client core is then no longer full (71% busy against 98%): the server's work per statement is what shrinks.
- **No gain for the 100-row reads** (`list`: 81.6k against 80.5k on three cores, 21.8k against 22.6k on one; the ranges overlap): producing the rows costs far more than the reply's `send()`.
- **The full path of an HTTP request gains little**, because there the HTTP side is the limit (`bench/db-path.sh`, results in `bench/results/db-path/`): with one giong worker and the database on two cores, 82.9k against 86.9k requests a second (ranges 79–96k and 75–93k), the database 84% busy against 93%; with two giong workers and the database on one core (`db-bound/`), 96.9k against 91.7k, p99 3.1 ms against 4.7 ms. Few requests arrive in the same tick for one connection there: 1.7 statements a batch on average, measured from the server's transaction count. One request at a time is unchanged (88–92 µs median).
- **Transaction-local settings.** The statements of a batch share one transaction, so a setting made with `set_config(.., true)` would apply to the other tasks' statements after it in the batch. A `SELECT` whose text calls `set_config` therefore runs alone; one that calls a function that makes such a setting (`set_config(.., true)` or `SET LOCAL` inside it) cannot be seen, so leave `batch_reads` off where row-level security or anything else is set up that way per request.
- What else changes for a statement in a batch is in the documentation of `Config::batch_reads`: in short, a write is refused in the batch (`25006`) and the statement is sent again alone; when a statement or the batch's commit fails, the batch is rolled back and every other statement of it is sent again alone; answers arrive when the batch ends; `now()` is the batch's start.
- MySQL has nothing like it: its protocol has no `Sync`, every statement gets its own reply, and giong-mysql already pipelines them.

Not measured: a server on another machine (network latency, where pipelining should matter more), writes, more than one client core, PostgreSQL versions other than 16. Results are in `bench/results/postgres/`; pool sizes other than 4 in `pool-size/`.

## Not there yet

`COPY`, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`, streaming a result one row at a time (a result is collected in full, up to `max_result_size`), arrays, `numeric`, `uuid`, `date` and the other types not listed above in binary form (read them as strings), channel binding (`SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS`), client certificates in the URL (`sslcert` and `sslkey` are refused; in code, give the connector one with `TlsConnector::client_auth`), several hosts with failover, running through PgBouncer without `max_prepared_statements`, and SASLprep normalization of non-ASCII passwords. The crate has had one independent review before 1.0, whose findings are fixed, but no security audit.

## Tests

`cargo test -p giong-postgres`: 70 tests against a real PostgreSQL server that the test binary starts for itself (a throwaway cluster from `initdb`, with users for SCRAM, MD5, clear text and TLS only, listening on a Unix socket, 127.0.0.1 and 127.0.0.2): every supported type in both directions; conversion errors; server errors and their fields; pipelining across tasks, and a failing statement in the middle of a pipeline; the statement cache, its bound, statement names an application took, and schema changes under cached statements, in and out of a transaction; notices and errors larger than the result limit; the result-size limit; the statement timeout, and leaving it to the server; cancel requests; a query dropped mid-flight; a connection the server terminates; transactions committed, rolled back and dropped, and a `COMMIT` turned into a rollback; no task or connection left behind after a client is dropped; TLS against the right and the wrong authority and host; each authentication method with the right and the wrong password, and `require_auth`; SCRAM keys derived once and off the worker; a server that answers the TLS request with extra bytes; a clear-text password never sent unencrypted; the connect timeout; and the pool (spreading statements, exclusive use and the rollback on return, even with `BEGIN` still in flight, the session reset on return and no reset for an unused connection, `get()` served in order while shared statements keep every connection busy, waiting, and waking when a dropped statement frees the connection, cancel tokens that stop working on return, idle and old connections closed, at most 1024 statements per connection at a time, replacing broken connections, connect errors, a slow statement not holding up the others, transaction and session statements refused on shared connections and a batch that leaves a transaction open; batched reads: each statement's own rows, one failing statement among good ones, `SELECT`s that write and lock rows, reads after writes, statements leaving the cache mid-batch, an error at a batch's commit, statements rolled back with their batch and run again, a statement that calls `set_config` kept out of batches (and one hidden in a function shared within its batch), the read-only guard prepared again after a `DEALLOCATE`, and no deadlock with a migration or with another batch taking locks in the opposite order). Two of them run a workload through PgBouncer in transaction mode, with the statement timeout left to the role, when PgBouncer is installed. 45 unit tests: the message encoder and parser, SCRAM against the RFC 7677 example, MD5 against RFC 1321, URLs, type conversions and how their errors name types, the statements the pool refuses and the ones it batches (never one that calls `set_config`), which errors are worth a retry, the old names of renamed methods, 42,000 random inputs for the message parser, the URL parser and SCRAM, and 300 sessions against a fake server answering with mutated replies (also the `session` fuzz target). 8 documentation examples.

The tests find PostgreSQL through `GIONG_PG_BIN`, `/usr/lib/postgresql/*/bin` or `PATH`, and skip when it is not installed, unless `GIONG_PG_REQUIRED=1` (CI sets it); PgBouncer likewise through `GIONG_PGBOUNCER_BIN`, `PATH` or `/usr/sbin`, and `GIONG_PGBOUNCER_REQUIRED=1`. Run as root, they start the server as the `postgres` user. They also pass under ThreadSanitizer and on the fallback io_uring setups (`scripts/check.sh tsan` and `fallback`).

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/giong-mysql/README.md -->

# giong-mysql

A MySQL and MariaDB client and connection pool for the [giong](https://giong.run/docs/giong.md) runtime. It speaks the client/server protocol itself (no libmysqlclient), encrypts with [`giong-tls`](https://giong.run/docs/giong-tls.md), and depends on nothing from the Tokio ecosystem.

```toml
[dependencies]
giong = "1.5.1"
giong-mysql = "1.5.1"
```

```rust,no_run
use giong_mysql::{Client, Config};

fn main() -> Result<(), giong_mysql::Error> {
    let config = Config::from_url("mysql://app:secret@localhost/shop")?;
    giong::block_on(async {
        let client = Client::connect(&config).await?;
        let rows = client
            .query("SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE price < ?", &[&100i32])
            .await?;
        for row in &rows {
            let id: i64 = row.get("id")?;
            let name: &str = row.get("name")?;
            println!("{id} {name}");
        }
        Ok(())
    })
}
```

In a service, make one `Pool` per worker. Nothing is shared between threads, so nothing is locked:

```rust,no_run
use giong_mysql::{Config, Pool};

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let config = Config::from_url("mysql://app:secret@db.internal/shop")?;
    giong::Builder::new().build()?.run(move |_worker| {
        let pool = Pool::new(config.clone(), 4);
        async move {
            // ... serve requests, each one calling pool.query(..) ...
            let id = pool
                .insert("INSERT INTO orders (customer) VALUES (?)", &[&42u64])
                .await
                .unwrap()
                .expect("orders has an AUTO_INCREMENT id");
            println!("order {id}");
        }
    })
}
```

## What it does

- **Pipelining across tasks.** Tasks that share a connection send their statements together, and one round trip answers all of them. A few connections serve hundreds of concurrent tasks, none of them waiting for a free connection. The usual MySQL clients (libmysqlclient, mysql_async, SQLx) have one statement in flight per connection.
- **Prepared statements, kept.** Every statement is prepared the first time a connection runs it and kept in a bounded cache (64 per connection by default), so from then on it takes one round trip, and parameters and rows travel in MySQL's binary format. The server's `max_prepared_stmt_count` bounds the statements of all its clients together; when it is reached anyway (error 1461), the connection's prepares take turns: each closes the statements not in use and tries again, pausing between tries, so a burst of new statements waits instead of failing; a prepare fails once none on the connection has succeeded for a second.
- **A pool per worker.** Statements that stand alone share connections; `pool.get()` takes one connection for a transaction, session settings or a slow statement. A connection comes back clean: if its session may have changed (a `SET`, a temporary table, a lock, a transaction left open), it is reset before anything else runs on it, without waiting for a round trip; one that ran only plain statements keeps its prepared statements. Tasks waiting in `get()` are served in order, and shared statements cannot keep them waiting: a connection is set aside for the oldest and handed over once the statements on it are answered. Transactions and session changes never run on the shared connections: the pool's own methods refuse `BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `SET`, `LOCK TABLES`, `CALL` and the like, and a batch that leaves a transaction open closes its connection rather than let the statements of other tasks run inside it. The pool steers new statements away from a connection whose oldest statement has been running for more than 5 ms, so a slow query does not hold up the fast ones behind it.
- **Transactions that cannot end silently.** In MySQL, a deadlock rolls the whole transaction back, so does a lock wait timeout when the server has `innodb_rollback_on_timeout` on, and `CREATE`, `ALTER` or `DROP` commits it; the statements after that run on their own, outside any transaction, without a word. Here they fail instead, and so does `commit`. So does a transaction in which a statement was given up (its future dropped by a timeout), since it may have run.
- **TLS on by default for remote hosts, always verified.** `caching_sha2_password` (MySQL 8's default) and `mysql_native_password`. A password is never sent where it could be read on the way (see [Passwords](#passwords)).
- **Errors that say what to do.** Every error has an `ErrorKind`; errors from the server carry MySQL's error number and SQLSTATE.
- **Finite limits everywhere.** Connecting, running a `SELECT`, waiting for a lock, the size of a result, the statement cache and waiting for the pool all have a limit by default, so nothing grows without bound. The one thing MySQL does not bound is a write that holds its locks and runs long; MariaDB bounds that too (see [Limits](#limits)).

## Connecting

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use giong_mysql::{Config, Error};

fn configs() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let config = Config::from_url("mysql://app:secret@db.internal:3306/shop?ssl-mode=VERIFY_IDENTITY")?;

    let same_place = Config::new()
        .host("db.internal")
        .user("app")
        .password("secret")
        .database("shop")
        .statement_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5));
    let _ = (config, same_place);
    Ok(())
}
```

A URL is `mysql://user:password@host:port/database?param=value`. The host can be an IPv6 address in brackets, or empty with the server's Unix socket in a `socket` parameter: `mysql://app@/shop?socket=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock` (in code, a host starting with `/` is a socket). The parameters understood are `ssl-mode`, `ssl-ca`, `socket`, `server-public-key-path`, `connect-timeout` (seconds) and `application-name`. Any other parameter is an error, not silently ignored.

Each connection starts its session with:

- the character set `utf8mb4` (`SET NAMES`), checked in the same round trip: a server that would store text in another character set without a word, because it ignores the handshake's or something undoes `SET NAMES`, is refused (`ErrorKind::Connect`);
- the time zone UTC (`+00:00`), so `TIMESTAMP` columns, `NOW()` and `SystemTime` agree;
- the statement timeout, as `max_execution_time` and `lock_wait_timeout` on MySQL, as `max_statement_time` and `lock_wait_timeout` on MariaDB;
- `autocommit` on, and the session tracker on, which tells the pool when a statement changed the session.

`Config::session_variable("sql_mode", "'STRICT_ALL_TABLES'")` sets other session variables; the ones above are refused there, except `lock_wait_timeout`. A value is one SQL expression: one holding a `;`, a comment, a backslash or a `,` outside quotes and parentheses is refused, so it cannot set a refused variable too. They are all set again whenever a pooled connection's session is reset.

**TLS.** Unless `Config::tls` or `ssl-mode` says otherwise:

| Where the server is | What happens |
|---|---|
| A Unix socket | No TLS. |
| A loopback address (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`) | No TLS. |
| Anywhere else | TLS, with the certificate checked against the certificate authorities installed on the machine and against the host name. |

`ssl-ca=/path/ca.pem` trusts only that authority instead of the machine's. `ssl-mode` is one of:

| `ssl-mode` | The certificate is checked against | In code |
|---|---|---|
| `DISABLED` | Nothing: no TLS. | `Tls::Disable` |
| `VERIFY_IDENTITY` | The authorities (`ssl-ca`, or the machine's) and the host name. | `Tls::Verify(TlsConnector::with_root_pem(..)?)` |
| `VERIFY_CA` | The authority in `ssl-ca`, which it needs, and not the host name. | `Tls::verify_ca(..)?` |
| `REQUIRED` | With `ssl-ca`, like `VERIFY_CA`, as in MySQL's own client. Without it, like `VERIFY_IDENTITY` against the machine's authorities, where MySQL's client checks nothing and anyone on the path could pose as the server. | |
| `PREFERRED` | Refused: it falls back to an unencrypted connection without saying so. | |

`VERIFY_CA` is for the certificates MySQL generates when it is installed, which name no host (`MySQL_Server_<version>_Auto_Generated_Server_Certificate`), so a host name check always fails: give it the server's own `ca.pem`, from its data directory. Use it only with an authority that signs for this server alone; with a public one, a certificate it issued for any name would pass. When TLS is requested and the server does not offer it, connecting fails.

### Passwords

`caching_sha2_password` logs in with a scramble of the password, which reveals nothing, once the server has the user in its cache. The first login after the server starts (or after `FLUSH PRIVILEGES`) needs the password itself. giong-mysql sends it:

| Connection | How the password goes |
|---|---|
| TLS, or a Unix socket | As it is, inside the encrypted or local connection. |
| No TLS, with `Config::server_public_key` (or `server-public-key-path`) | Encrypted with that RSA key. |
| No TLS, to a loopback address | Encrypted with the RSA key the server sends when asked. Nobody can sit in between on this machine's loopback. |
| No TLS, to another machine, no key configured | Not at all: connecting fails with `ErrorKind::Auth`. Asking the server for its key over the network would let anyone in between replace it and read the password. |

`sha256_password` and clear-text plugins are answered only over TLS or a Unix socket. LDAP, Kerberos and PAM plugins are not supported.

## API

| | |
|---|---|
| `Client::connect(&config)` | Opens a connection: TCP or Unix socket, TLS, authentication, the session settings, all within `connect_timeout`. |
| `client.query(sql, &[&a, &b])` | All the rows, as `Vec<Row>`. Parameters are `?`. A stored procedure (`CALL`) gives the rows of its first result. |
| `client.query_one(..)`, `query_opt(..)` | Exactly one row (`ErrorKind::RowCount` otherwise); at most one. |
| `client.execute(..)` | The number of rows inserted, updated (matched, including rows already holding the new values) or deleted. |
| `client.insert(..)` | The `AUTO_INCREMENT` id an `INSERT` generated (of its first row), or `None` if it generated none; the statement ran either way. |
| `client.batch_execute(sql)` | Several statements separated by `;`, with no parameters and no results, stopping at the first error. For migrations and setup. |
| `client.transaction()` | Starts a transaction and borrows the client mutably until it ends. `tx.commit()` or `tx.rollback()`; dropping the transaction rolls it back. A transaction the server ended early (deadlock, lock wait timeout with `innodb_rollback_on_timeout`, DDL), or one with a statement given up, refuses further statements, and its `commit` fails. |
| `client.reset_session()` | Resets the session the way the pool does when a connection comes back: rolls back, releases locks, drops temporary tables and variables, and sets the session up again. For a stored function or trigger that takes a named lock or sets a user variable, which the server does not report. |
| `client.cancel_token()` | A `CancelToken` whose `cancel()` runs `KILL QUERY` over a separate connection, stopping the statement running now. It goes to the address the connection reached and only if the server there is the same one, so behind a load balancer it cannot stop another session's statement. A token taken from a pooled connection (`pool.get()`) stops working, sending nothing, once the connection goes back to the pool, and a connection that goes back while such a request is on its way is closed rather than lent to another task. |
| `client.server_version()`, `client.connection_id()` | What the server said when connecting; the id is the one `KILL` and `SHOW PROCESSLIST` use. |
| `client.is_closed()`, `client.in_flight()` | Whether the connection is closed; how many requests are waiting for their answer. |
| `row.get::<T>(column)` | A column by position or name, converted to `T` (see [Types](#types)). Borrowed types (`&str`, `&[u8]`) borrow from the row. |
| `row.is_null(column)`, `row.columns()`, `row.len()` | Whether a value is `NULL`; the columns' names and types; how many there are. |
| `Pool::new(config, max_size)` | A pool for the current worker. Connections are opened when needed, up to `max_size`. Size it to the database server's cores, shared among the workers (see [Performance](#performance)). |
| `.wait_timeout(duration)` | How long `get()` and the statement methods wait when every connection is taken, 5 s by default. |
| `.idle_timeout(duration)`, `.max_lifetime(duration)` | Close a connection unused for this long (10 min by default); replace one older than this (30 min, less up to 10% so that connections opened together are not replaced together). |
| `pool.query(..)` and the other statement methods | Run on the least busy connection, pipelined with other tasks' statements. |
| `pool.get()` | A `PooledClient` for this task alone, which derefs to `Client`. For transactions, session settings and statements known to be slow. Its session is reset when it comes back, if it may have changed. |
| `pool.stats()` | Connections open, taken, being opened, set aside for `get()`; requests in flight; tasks waiting; and counters for connections opened, connect errors, wait timeouts, sessions reset, prepares refused for `max_prepared_stmt_count` and connections recycled. |

A `Client` belongs to the worker that opened it (it is not `Send`, like everything in giong). Its methods take `&self`, so tasks share one by cloning an `Rc` or by holding a reference, and their statements are pipelined.

## Types

Parameters are sent as the MySQL type that holds them exactly; the server converts them to the column's type as it would a literal.

| Rust | Parameter | Columns it reads |
|---|---|---|
| `i8` ... `i64`, `u8` ... `u64` | `TINYINT` ... `BIGINT` (`UNSIGNED`) | Any integer column and `YEAR`, when the value fits; a `DECIMAL` that is a whole number |
| `bool` | `TINYINT` 1 or 0 | An integer column holding 0 or 1 |
| `f32`, `f64` | `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE` | `FLOAT` (both), `DOUBLE` (`f64`) |
| `&str`, `String` | A string in `utf8mb4` | `CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT`, `ENUM`, `SET`, `JSON`, `DECIMAL`; `String` also `DATE`, `TIME` and `DATETIME` as text |
| `&[u8]`, `Vec<u8>`, `[u8; N]` | A binary string | Every string and blob column, `BIT`, `GEOMETRY` |
| `SystemTime` | `DATETIME(6)` in UTC | `DATETIME`, `TIMESTAMP` |
| `giong_mysql::Bits` | | `BIT` |
| `Option<T>` | `NULL` or a value | `NULL` or a value |

Conversions never lose anything silently: a value that does not fit, a binary column read as text, or a `NULL` read into a type that cannot hold it fails with an error that names the column and the types that would work. Pass a `DECIMAL` as a string (`"19.99"`) to keep it exact. Implement `ToSql` and `FromSql` for your own types.

## Errors

`Error` is cheap to clone, implements `std::error::Error`, and converts into `io::Error`. `error.kind()` says what went wrong. Each kind has a giong error code, shown in front of the message and linked to its page in [docs/errors](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md) (`GIONG-E3104: ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1' for key 'users.PRIMARY'. See …`); after `?` into an `io::Error`, `giong::error::code(&err)` finds it:

| `ErrorKind` | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Config` | [E3101](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3101.md) | The configuration or URL is not valid, or the server refused a session variable. |
| `Connect` | [E3102](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3102.md) | Name resolution, TCP, TLS, or the connect timeout. Also an unknown database (1049), a server older than MySQL 8.0 or MariaDB 10.6, a session whose character set is not `utf8mb4`, and a cancel request that reached another server. |
| `Auth` | [E3103](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3103.md) | The server refused the credentials, asked for a plugin this crate does not support, or would have needed the password where it could be read. |
| `Db` | [E3104](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3104.md) | The server reported an error for the statement; `error.server_code()` is MySQL's error number (1062 for a duplicate key, 1213 for a deadlock...) and `error.db()` has the SQLSTATE too. |
| `Type` | [E3105](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3105.md) | A value could not be converted between Rust and MySQL, or the number of parameters is wrong. The message names the parameter or column and suggests the Rust type to use. |
| `RowCount` | [E3106](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3106.md) | `query_one` found no row or several, `query_opt` several. |
| `TooLarge` | [E3107](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3107.md) | The result was larger than `max_result_size`. The connection stays usable. |
| `Closed` | [E3108](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3108.md) | The connection is closed. A `Pool` replaces it by itself. |
| `PoolTimeout` | [E3109](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3109.md) | No pooled connection became free within `wait_timeout`. |
| `Protocol` | [E3110](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3110.md) | The server sent something this crate cannot understand. The connection is closed. |
| `Statement` | [E3111](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E3111.md) | Refused before sending: a transaction statement, or one that changes the session (`SET`, `USE`, `LOCK TABLES`, a temporary table, `GET_LOCK`, a user variable), on the connections a `Pool` shares. Use `pool.get()`, and `transaction()`. |

`error.is_transient()` is true for errors worth retrying after a pause: connecting, a closed connection, a pool wait timeout, and the server's deadlock (1213), lock wait timeout (1205), too many connections (1040, 1203), shutdown (1053), read-only mode (1290 naming `--read-only`, 1792, 1836) and a killed connection (1927, MariaDB). Retry a whole transaction, not its failed statement.

An error from the server affects only its own statement: the statements that other tasks pipelined on the same connection get their own results.

## Limits

| Setting | Default | What happens at the limit |
|---|---|---|
| `Config::connect_timeout` | 10 s | `ErrorKind::Connect`, "connect timeout". |
| `Config::statement_timeout` | 30 s | On MySQL, sent as the session's `max_execution_time`, so the server stops a `SELECT` that runs too long (error 3024), and as `lock_wait_timeout`, so a statement waiting for a table or metadata lock gives up (1205). A write waiting for a row lock gives up after `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` (50 s by default); one that holds its locks and runs long is not stopped. On MariaDB, sent as `max_statement_time`, which stops every statement (1969), and as `lock_wait_timeout`. |
| `Config::max_result_size` | 64 MiB of row data | `ErrorKind::TooLarge`; the rest of the result is read and thrown away. |
| `Config::statement_cache_capacity` | 64 per connection | The least recently used statement is closed. 0 prepares and closes every statement each time. The server's `max_prepared_stmt_count` (16,382 by default) bounds the statements of all its clients: processes × workers × pool size × this must stay below it (64 allows 255 connections). At that limit (error 1461), the connection's prepares take turns, closing its unused statements and trying again, and fail once none has succeeded for a second. |
| `Pool::wait_timeout` | 5 s | `ErrorKind::PoolTimeout`. |
| `Pool::idle_timeout` | 10 min | The connection is closed. |
| `Pool::max_lifetime` | 30 min, less up to 10% | The connection is closed once no statement uses it (one taken with `get()`, when it comes back), and a new one is opened when needed. |

Values over 16 MiB are split into packets and joined again, both ways. The server's `max_allowed_packet` (64 MiB by default) limits the size of a statement with its parameters, and of a row.

## Performance

Measured with `bench/mysql.sh` against mysql_async 0.36.2 and SQLx 0.8.6, each with its own pool (Tokio 1.54, current-thread runtime). Each client runs on one core; the same MySQL 8.0.46 server runs on the other three cores of a 4-vCPU virtual machine (Xeon 2.1 GHz, Linux 6.18), reached over TCP on 127.0.0.1. 64 tasks issue statements back to back: `point` reads one row by primary key, `list` reads 100 rows, and every column of every row is decoded (`i64`, two strings, a date and time). The figures are medians of 5 rounds of 5 s (3 rounds for the other pool sizes), with the range in brackets.

A pool, on one client core:

| Client | Connections | `point` statements/s | p99 | `list` statements/s | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **giong-mysql** | 3 | **150.7k** (142–158k) | **0.81 ms** | **38.9k** (36–40k) | **3.4 ms** |
| giong-mysql | 4 | 152.1k (134–157k) | 4.4 ms | 38.3k (37–41k) | 6.5 ms |
| SQLx | 4 | 17.7k (17–18k) | 4.8 ms | 7.6k (7.0–8.4k) | 13.2 ms |
| SQLx | 64, its best | 29.3k (26–30k) | 3.9 ms | 10.4k (9.0–11.7k) | 9.1 ms |
| mysql_async | 4, its best | 17.1k (16–18k) | 6.4 ms | 9.5k (8.7–10.4k) | 11.2 ms |
| mysql_async, default pool settings | 4 | 11.5k (9.9–12.7k) | 8.7 ms | 6.4k (5.9–7.2k) | 14.2 ms |

- **Against the best of the others (SQLx with 64 connections): 5.1× the point lookups and 3.7× the 100-row reads, at a fifth to a third of the p99.** SQLx's client core is the limit (99–100% busy). giong-mysql sends the statements of all 64 tasks in a few writes and reads their answers in a few reads; here the server is its limit (its three cores 94% busy), not the client core (74–89%).
- **mysql_async** is not limited by its core (66–90% busy) and does best with 4 connections: with 16 it does 16.8k point lookups, with 64 13.7k at a p99 of 28 ms. By default its pool resets every connection it takes back (`COM_RESET_CONNECTION`, which also drops the connection's prepared statements); that costs it a third of its throughput (the last row). The other mysql_async rows turn it off.
- **Size the pool to the database's cores.** With more connections than the server has cores (4 on 3 here), one server thread at a time waits for a core, and the statements pipelined on its connection wait with it: the same throughput, but a p99 of 4.4 ms instead of 0.81. 8 connections give 161.6k at a p99 of 8.2 ms; 2 connections leave a server core idle, 87.9k. With several workers, the connections of all their pools add up. Statements that wait on disk or on locks need more connections than this.
- **One connection shared by every task:** 26.6k point lookups and 10.8k 100-row reads, about what SQLx does with 64 connections, using 29–35% of the client core. The single server thread is the limit. Neither of the others can share a connection between tasks.

Not measured: a server on another machine (network latency, where pipelining should matter more), writes, more than one client core, MySQL versions other than 8.0.46. Results are in `bench/results/mysql/`; pool sizes other than 4 in `pool-size/`.

## Not there yet

Streaming a result one row at a time (a result is collected in full, up to `max_result_size`) and cursors, the result sets after the first from a `CALL`, `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` (the server is never sent a file), compression, several hosts with failover, MariaDB's own extensions (its `client_ed25519` login among them), and authentication plugins other than those above. MySQL 8.0 and later and MariaDB 10.6 and later are supported; older versions are refused when connecting.

## Tests

`cargo test -p giong-mysql`: 74 tests against a real MySQL or MariaDB server that the test binary starts for itself (a throwaway data directory from `mysqld --initialize-insecure` or `mariadb-install-db`, with a user for each authentication plugin and path and one that requires TLS, listening on a Unix socket, 127.0.0.1 and 127.0.0.2), and a second one set up the way some production servers are (`init_connect` setting latin1, `innodb_rollback_on_timeout` on, the certificates MySQL generates itself): every supported type in both directions; conversion errors that name the column; server errors and their fields; pipelining across tasks, and a failing statement in the middle of a pipeline; the statement cache and its bound, counted on the server, and a cached statement after a schema change; values of 16 MiB and more, both ways; the result-size limit; the statement timeout; `KILL QUERY` through a cancel token; a query dropped mid-flight; a connection the server kills; a stored procedure with two results; `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` refused; transactions committed, rolled back, dropped, ended by DDL and by a deadlock; no task or connection left behind after a client is dropped; TLS against the right and the wrong authority and host; `caching_sha2_password` over a socket, TCP and TLS, with RSA (the key asked for on loopback, or configured), and from a non-loopback address (through a forwarder on this machine's network address) where only the fast path may log in; `mysql_native_password`; `sha256_password` only over TLS; fake servers that ask for the password over the network, lack TLS, or predate MySQL 8; the connect timeout; and the pool (spreading statements, exclusive use and the rollback on return, even with `BEGIN` still in flight, waiting, and waking when a dropped statement frees the connection, replacing broken connections, connect errors, a slow statement not holding up the others, transaction statements refused on shared connections and a batch that leaves a transaction open); a connection taken and given back with session variables, a temporary table, user variables, `autocommit` off, `LOCK TABLES` and `GET_LOCK` comes back clean, and one that ran only plain statements keeps its prepared statements; session statements refused on shared connections, and a reset after a shared batch or trigger that changed the session; a failed reset closes the connection; `get()` not starved by 32 tasks of shared statements, waiting tasks served in order, a connection set aside for a task that gave up going back, idle connections closed, and old ones replaced under load and when they come back from `get()`, and lifetimes too long for the clock; text stored as `utf8mb4` where the server would make it latin1; the server-wide limit on prepared statements reached; a cancel request through a round-robin balancer that must not stop another server's statement; lock wait timeouts with and without the rollback of the transaction; a write waiting for a table lock bounded by the statement timeout; a statement given up inside a transaction stopping the commit; and `VERIFY_CA` with the certificates MySQL generates. 44 unit tests: packets and their splitting, the scrambles checked the way the server checks them, RSA-OAEP decrypted by the `openssl` command, URLs, type conversions and how their errors name types, the certificate check of `VERIFY_CA`, the versions refused, which errors are worth a retry and the old name of `server_code`, and random inputs for the packet parsers, the framing, rows of every column type, URLs, key files and the connection's state machine (3,000 sessions against a scripted server that sends mutated answers). 8 documentation examples. The fuzz targets in `fuzz/` cover the same parsers and the state machine (`session`) with coverage guidance.

The tests find `mysqld` through `GIONG_MYSQL_BIN` (the directory that holds it), `/usr/sbin` or `PATH`, and the `mysql` client next to it or on `PATH`. They skip when MySQL is not installed, unless `GIONG_MYSQL_REQUIRED=1` (CI sets it). They also pass under ThreadSanitizer and on the fallback io_uring setups (`scripts/check.sh tsan` and `fallback`). They have passed against MySQL 8.0.46 and MariaDB 10.11 here; CI runs them against MySQL 8.0, 8.4 and 9.1 and MariaDB 10.6, 10.11, 11.4 and 11.8. For MariaDB, point `GIONG_MYSQL_BIN` at the directory that holds `mariadbd`.
