<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/guides/coding-agents.md -->

# Build with a coding agent

Gióng is made for code that agents write: one obvious way to do each job, errors that say how to fix them, and a `giong` command that answers in JSON. This page is the setup and the loop to give an agent, whether you type every prompt or let it run on its own.

## Set the project up once

`giong new` writes a project that already teaches agents how to work on it. For a project you already have, run the same step on its own:

```sh
giong new api                 # a new project (a users API on SQLite), with the files below
giong ai init                 # an existing project: the same files, nothing else touched
```

It writes:

| File | Read by |
|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` | Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini and most other agents: the Gióng rules and this project's commands |
| `CLAUDE.md` | Claude Code; it imports `AGENTS.md` |
| `.cursor/rules/giong.mdc` | Cursor |
| `.claude/skills/giong/` | Agents that load skills: the Gióng skill of this release |
| `.mcp.json` | Agents that speak MCP: the `giong` server (`giong mcp`) |

`giong upgrade` runs it again when it moves the project to a new release; run it yourself after moving giong by hand. In a file you wrote, it replaces only its own marked block; in `.mcp.json` it adds its server and keeps everything else.

## The loop an agent follows

One project has one runner, and the agent drives it with these commands only:

```sh
giong dev --background          # once: builds, serves on 127.0.0.1, returns when it answers
# ... edit the code: the runner rebuilds on every save and swaps the new build in ...
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
giong dev status --json         # is it up, where, and why not (failure: code, cause, last lines, fix)
giong dev logs --lines 50       # what the service printed
giong check --json              # compiler, clippy and giong's own checks: run before calling it done
giong fix                       # applies the fixes that need no judgement
giong test                      # the tests, on io_uring and on epoll
giong dev stop                  # at the end: the service, and the database giong started
```

What the agent must not do while developing: `cargo run`, `cargo build --release`, start Docker or a container itself, or open a second terminal to run the service. Each of those starts a second copy that fights the runner for the port. A change that does not compile, or that compiles but does not start (a panic at start-up, a port it cannot bind), stops the service instead of leaving an older build answering: the agent never tests code that is not in the files. Requests are refused until the code works, and `giong dev status --json` says why: `state` is `failed` and `failure` holds the code (`GIONG-E5009` for the compiler, `GIONG-E5017` for a service that stopped, `GIONG-E5014` for a port in use, `GIONG-E5018` for one that never listened), the cause, the compiler's errors or the service's last lines in `detail`, and the fix. The agent fixes the code and saves; the runner builds and serves again by itself.

## Connect the agent to giong over MCP

`.mcp.json` already names the server for agents that read it. In Claude Code, by hand:

```sh
claude mcp add giong -- giong mcp
```

Every command that only reads is a tool: `check`, `doctor`, `explain`, `routes`, `top`, `dev` for `status` and `logs`. Commands that change the project (`fix`, `dev --background`, `dev stop`, ...) are tools only when you start the server with `giong mcp --allow-writes`. Some are never tools, whatever the flag: emptying or removing a database, `clean --all`, reading a secret value, pushing an image.

While `giong dev` runs the service, the agent can also ask the service itself, through [giong-mcp](https://giong.run/docs/giong-mcp.md), which task blocks a worker, which line spawned the tasks that keep growing, and how full the pools are. That is faster and more certain than guessing from the code.

## Read what giong reports

Every command takes `--json` and answers with one document. Each problem is a finding with a code, the place in the source, the cause and the fix:

```json
{"command": "check", "ok": false,
 "findings": [{"code": "GIONG-E5006", "severity": "warning",
               "title": "std::fs blocks the worker inside an async function",
               "fix": "...", "file": "src/main.rs", "line": 14, "column": 19}]}
```

The exit status is 0 when nothing is wrong, 1 when a finding is an error, and 2 when the command could not run. Every code has a page: `giong explain GIONG-E5006` prints it without the network, and the [error index](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md) lists them all.

## Give the agent the documentation

- `https://giong.run/llms.txt`: what an agent needs first, with links to everything else.
- `https://giong.run/llms-full.txt`: every README, the guides and every error page in one file.
- Every page of giong.run is also Markdown: add `.md` to its address, or press **Copy for agent**.
- **Copy prompt** on any page copies the rules and that page, ready to paste with your task.

## A first prompt

```text
This is a Rust service on Gióng. Read AGENTS.md first.
Start it with `giong dev --background` if `giong dev status` says it is not running,
then: <what to build or fix>.
Check your work with curl against 127.0.0.1, then `giong check --json` and `giong test`.
Do not use cargo run, a release build or Docker. Stop with `giong dev stop` when done.
```

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/guides/safe-defaults.md -->

# Safe defaults of the dev kit

The `giong` command runs code, holds secrets and opens ports on the machine you work on. It is built so that the default is the safe choice, and every way out of it is a flag you type. This page lists each default, what it protects and how to change it.

## Nothing listens beyond this machine

- A new project's `.env.example` sets `LISTEN=127.0.0.1:<port>`; only its Dockerfile sets `0.0.0.0`, for production.
- `giong dev` serves an address of every interface (`0.0.0.0`, `[::]`) on loopback instead, with the warning `GIONG-E5024`. `--lan` keeps the address, to reach the service from a phone or another computer.
- The dashboard listens on `127.0.0.1` only and answers only a loopback `Host`.

## The dashboard needs its token

Each `giong dashboard` or `giong dev --ui` makes a random token, printed as part of its address (`http://127.0.0.1:7700/#t=...`). Every API call needs it in the `X-Giong-Dashboard` header, or gets `403` with `GIONG-E5051`. The token comes after `#`, so no request line, log or `Referer` carries it, and the page takes it out of the address bar once read. A web page, another program or another user on the machine cannot read the dashboard or send requests through it.

## Recorded requests keep secrets out

`giong record save` writes real requests as test cases that are meant to be committed, so:

- Redacted headers, and fields whose names say secret (`password`, `token`, `api_key`, `client_secret`, `card_number`, `cvv` and the like) in a query, a form or a JSON body, become `{{env:GIONG_RECORD_<NAME>}}` and are read from the environment when the cases run. The same fields in answers become `{{string}}`.
- A value that still looks like a secret, such as a card number (by the Luhn check), a JWT or a value under a secret name, stops the save with `GIONG-E5050`, and nothing is written. `--keep-secrets` saves anyway, with warnings, for test values such as the `4242 4242 4242 4242` card.
- giong-web's `Record` middleware redacts the same names as `[redacted]` (`redact_field` and `keep_field` change the list), and it is compiled out of release builds unless the `dev` feature is on (`GIONG-E1213`).

## Agents read; they change things only when you allow it

`giong mcp` serves the commands that only read. Commands that change the project need `giong mcp --allow-writes`. Emptying or removing a database, `giong clean --all`, printing a secret value (`giong env get`, `--reveal`) and pushing an image are never tools.

## Development code stays out of production

`giong dev` hands its listening sockets to the service it starts, so a new build can take over without refusing a connection. The runtime takes a socket only from the `giong dev` that started it, and only in debug builds or with giong's `dev` feature, which `giong dev --release` and `--prod-like` turn on for their own builds. A release build without it refuses to start under `giong dev` instead of taking the socket.

## Secrets stay in .env, and .env stays on this machine

- `giong db up` starts each database with a random password and writes its URL to `.env`, which it makes readable by you only and lists in `.gitignore`.
- Each checkout gets its own container, so two copies of a project never share a database; a container giong did not record is refused with `GIONG-E5049` instead of guessing its password.
- `.env` is read in development only (`giong dev`, `giong test`); in production the service takes its settings from the environment. `giong env show` masks secret values, and a value only the process environment sets shows as `*** (set in the environment)`; `--reveal` prints them.
- `giong db` ignores an entry in `.giong/db.json` that `giong db up` could not have written (another container runtime, another checkout's container, an unusual image or user), with the warning `GIONG-E5048`, so an edited file cannot point it at something else.
- `giong db`, `giong env` and `giong bench` refuse to read or write `.env`, `.gitignore` or their `.giong` files through a symbolic link, and `giong image --add` takes a link only to a file inside the project.

## The install script checks what it downloads

`curl -fsSL https://giong.run/install.sh | sh` downloads the release binary from GitHub, checks its SHA-256 and puts it in `~/.giong/bin` without asking for root. `GIONG_VERSION` pins a version.

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/guides/database.md -->

# Use a database

A local database for development in one command, forward-only migrations, and the pool pattern every giong service uses. PostgreSQL is shown; MySQL and Redis work the same way. A project from `giong new` starts on [SQLite](#sqlite), which needs nothing installed or started.

## Start one for development

```sh
giong db up            # PostgreSQL, MySQL or Redis in Docker or Podman, for the crates the project uses
giong db new add_users # writes migrations/0002_add_users.sql
giong db migrate       # applies what is new
giong db status        # what is applied
```

`giong db up` gives the database a random password, a free port and a volume, and writes `DATABASE_URL` (or `REDIS_URL`) into `.env`, which only you can read and git ignores. Each checkout of the project gets its own container. `giong dev stop` stops it with the service and keeps its data; `giong db down` removes it, and `--volumes` deletes the data too. The [`giong db` page](https://giong.run/docs/cli/db.md) has every subcommand.

## Migrations

Migrations are plain SQL files, `migrations/NNNN_name.sql`, applied in order and never undone:

- Each PostgreSQL file runs in one transaction, unless its first line is `-- giong:no-transaction` (for `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and the like).
- Each applied file is recorded with its SHA-256; changing a file that was already applied is refused. Write a new file instead.
- A file that fails names its line.
- With a `DATABASE_URL` of your own (staging, production), `giong db migrate` and `giong db status` work on that database.

## One pool per worker

Build the pool inside each worker's future, from the environment. Nothing is shared between threads, so nothing is locked:

```rust
use giong_postgres::{Config, Pool};

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL").expect("DATABASE_URL");
    let config = Config::from_url(&url).expect("DATABASE_URL");
    giong::Builder::new().shutdown_on_signals(true).build()?.run(move |_worker| {
        let pool = Pool::new(config.clone(), 4);
        async move {
            let row = pool.query_one("SELECT count(*) FROM orders", &[]).await.unwrap();
            let n: i64 = row.get(0).unwrap();
            println!("{n} orders");
        }
    })
}
```

- `pool.query(..)`, `query_one`, `execute` share connections between tasks and pipeline their statements: a few connections serve hundreds of tasks.
- Transactions, `SET`, `LISTEN` and temporary tables need a connection of their own: `let mut conn = pool.get().await?;`. The pool's shared methods refuse them before sending anything. When `conn` is dropped, an open transaction is rolled back and the session is reset.
- Size the pool for the transactions that run at once, plus one. Spread the database server's cores over the workers rather than giving each worker many connections.
- Every wait has a limit by default: connecting, a statement, the pool (`GIONG-E3009` when it runs out).

The [giong-postgres](https://giong.run/docs/giong-postgres.md), [giong-mysql](https://giong.run/docs/giong-mysql.md) and [giong-redis](https://giong.run/docs/giong-redis.md) pages have the whole API, the types and the limits.

## Test against the real database

`giong test` reads `.env`, so the tests see the `DATABASE_URL` that `giong db up` wrote. A project from `giong new --db postgres` already has an end to end test that does this, and a CI workflow that starts the same database as a service.

## SQLite

`giong new api` keeps its users in SQLite: the file `data/api.db`, made at the first start, with SQLite compiled in by rusqlite (feature `bundled`). Nothing to install, nothing to start, and `giong db migrate`, `status` and `reset --yes` work on the file (through the `sqlite3` shell).

SQLite is a C library that does its reads and writes in the calling thread, so a query on a worker holds up every connection of that worker. The project's `src/db.rs` runs every query on giong's blocking lane instead:

```rust
let user = state
    .db
    .read(move |c| Ok(c.query_row(SELECT_ONE, [id], User::from_row).optional()?))
    .await?;
```

- `db.read(..)` runs the closure with one of a few read connections, `db.write(..)` with the one write connection, both on `giong::spawn_blocking` threads. The closure gets what it needs moved in and gives back owned values.
- The file is in WAL mode: reads run side by side and while a write runs. SQLite runs one write at a time whatever the number of connections, so writes queue for the write connection instead of failing with `database is locked`; `c.transaction()` inside `write` makes several statements one change.
- One `Db` is shared by every worker (it is the one thing a giong service shares, since SQLite allows one writer per file). One copy of the service owns the file: for several copies or machines, `giong new --db postgres` writes the same service on PostgreSQL.
- The tests open a file of their own each in the temporary directory, so they always run and never share rows.

## Not with sqlx or tokio-postgres

Crates that need the Tokio runtime (sqlx, tokio-postgres's runtime, most ORMs built on them) panic on a giong worker with "there is no reactor running". Use the giong crate for each database.

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/guides/testing.md -->

# Test a service

Three kinds of tests cover a giong service: plain unit tests of async code, handler tests without a socket, and recorded requests replayed against the running service. `giong test` runs the first two the way CI and production will see them.

## Async code in a plain test

There are no macros. Run a future in a test with `giong::block_on`:

```rust
#[test]
fn sums() {
    let n = giong::block_on(async { 1 + 1 });
    assert_eq!(n, 2);
}
```

## A handler without a socket

A giong-web app answers a request in memory, so a test checks the status and the coded error without binding a port:

```rust
use giong_web::{Error, Req, Request, Response, Router};

async fn get_user(req: Req<()>) -> Result<Response, Error> {
    let id: u64 = req.param("id")?;
    Ok(Response::text(format!("user {id}")))
}

#[test]
fn rejects_a_bad_id() {
    let app = Router::new().get("/users/{id}", get_user).build(());
    let req = Request::from_bytes(b"GET /users/abc HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: t\r\n\r\n").unwrap();
    let resp = giong::block_on(app.handle(req));
    assert_eq!(resp.status(), 400);
    assert_eq!(giong_web::Error::of(&resp).unwrap().code(), "GIONG-E1205");
}
```

## Run them with giong test

```sh
giong test                 # cargo test with .env, then again with GIONG_DRIVER=epoll on Linux
giong test --quick         # once
giong test -- users        # arguments after -- go to cargo test
```

- Each failing test is a finding (`GIONG-E5083`) that names the driver it failed on and what it printed.
- The second run on epoll matters: a container without io_uring (Docker's default seccomp profile, gVisor) runs on epoll.
- A run longer than `--timeout` (1800 s by default) is stopped with every process it started, naming the tests still running.
- `--nextest` uses cargo-nextest. Every flag: [`giong test`](https://giong.run/docs/cli/test.md).

## Real requests as tests

Add giong-web's `Record` middleware, use the service while `giong dev` runs, then keep the requests you want:

```sh
giong record list --status 4xx       # what was answered
giong record save last --name signup # tests/recorded/signup.json
giong record replay                  # send them again and compare, field by field
```

Ids, times and tokens the service made become placeholders, an id one request returns and a later one uses is captured, and secrets stay out of the file. A difference fails like a test (`GIONG-E5066`), so `giong record replay` belongs in CI next to `giong test`. Details: [`giong record`](https://giong.run/docs/cli/record.md) and [Safe defaults](https://giong.run/docs/guides/safe-defaults.md).

## In CI

A project from `giong new` has a GitHub Actions workflow that starts the databases it needs as services and runs its tests. Keep `giong check --json` in it too: it fails on the mistakes giong knows, such as a blocking call on a worker.

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/guides/ship.md -->

# Ship a service

From a project that passes `giong check` and `giong test` to an image running in production: measure the change, build the image, and set the few things production needs.

## Measure before you ship

```sh
giong bench --against main             # this checkout against main, round by round
giong bench http://127.0.0.1:8080/users/7 --rate auto
```

`giong bench` sends load at a fixed rate and counts each request's latency from when it was due, so a stall is charged to every request behind it. `--against` builds both versions and alternates them; `--max-regression 5` fails only when the change is slower in every round of at least three. The load generator shares the machine with the service: numbers to publish come from two machines. Every flag: [`giong bench`](https://giong.run/docs/cli/bench.md).

## Build the image

```sh
giong image --tag shop:1.0              # an OCI image, without Docker or a Dockerfile
giong image --push ghcr.io/owner/shop:1.0
```

One layer with the release binary at `/app`, CA certificates and a nonroot user, no shell. It is static when the musl target is installed (`rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`); the same source gives the same digest. `--add static,migrations` adds folders, `--load` hands the image to Docker or Podman. A project from `giong new` also has a Dockerfile, for a pipeline that wants one.

## What production needs

- **The address.** Development listens on `127.0.0.1`. In production set `LISTEN=0.0.0.0:8080` (the Dockerfile from `giong new` does).
- **Settings from the environment.** `.env` is for development only; give production its variables (`DATABASE_URL`, secrets) from the platform. `giong env check` lists what `.env.example` expects.
- **Graceful shutdown.** Services from `giong new` shut down gracefully on `SIGTERM`. Give the platform's stop timeout a few seconds more than your slowest request.
- **Migrations.** Run `giong db migrate` against the production `DATABASE_URL` before the new version starts.

## io_uring in containers

Docker's and Kubernetes' default seccomp profiles block io_uring, so giong runs on its epoll driver there by itself, with no settings. To use io_uring, allow its three system calls with the profile in [Deployment](https://giong.run/docs/deployment.md), which also covers the locked-memory limit on newer kernels and restarting on the same port.

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/guides/from-tokio.md -->

# Coming from Tokio

What changes when a Tokio service moves to giong: the runtime model, the names, and the crate for each job. Most code keeps its shape; the differences are where tasks run and who owns buffers.

## The model

- **Thread per core.** Each worker owns its ring, its tasks and its buffers. A task never moves to another thread, so futures need not be `Send`.
- **State per worker.** Build listeners, routers, pools and clients inside each worker's future. Per-worker state is an `Rc<RefCell<T>>`, never borrowed across an `.await`, rather than an `Arc<Mutex<T>>`.
- **Never block a worker.** One blocked call stops every task on that worker. Use `giong::fs`, `giong::net` and `giong::time`; heavy work goes to `std::thread::spawn` and comes back through `giong::sync::oneshot`.
- **Buffers by value.** The kernel uses a buffer after the call, so it is passed in and handed back: `stream.write_all(buf).await` returns `(io::Result<()>, buf)`.

## Name for name

| Tokio | giong |
|---|---|
| `#[tokio::main]` | `giong::Builder::new().build()?.run(\|_\| async { .. })` or `giong::block_on` |
| `tokio::spawn` | `giong::spawn` (stays on the worker; no `Send`); `Handle::spawn_on` or `spawn_balanced` for other workers |
| `tokio::join!`, `select!` | `futures::join!`, `futures::select!` |
| `spawn_blocking` | `std::thread::spawn` + `giong::sync::oneshot` |
| `Arc<Mutex<T>>` in handlers | `Rc<RefCell<T>>` per worker, or a channel |
| `tokio::time::interval` | a loop around `giong::time::sleep_until(next)` |
| `tokio::signal::ctrl_c()` | `Builder::shutdown_on_signals(true)` + `giong::shutdown_signal().await` |
| `read(&mut buf)` / `write_all(&buf)` | `recv()` lends a buffer; `write_all(buf)` returns `(result, buf)` |
| `TcpListener::bind("localhost:8080")` | `TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080")`: IP addresses only (`GIONG-E0100`) |

`giong::sync` has `mpsc` and `oneshot`. Tokio's `sync` module (`Semaphore`, `Notify`, `watch`, `broadcast`) needs no Tokio runtime and works on giong as it is.

## The crate for each job

| Job | Instead of | Use |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP server | hyper, axum | [giong-http](https://giong.run/docs/giong-http.md) |
| Routing, JSON, middleware | axum, tower-http | [giong-web](https://giong.run/docs/giong-web.md) |
| HTTP client | reqwest | giong-http with feature `client` |
| TLS | tokio-rustls | [giong-tls](https://giong.run/docs/giong-tls.md) |
| gRPC | tonic | [giong-grpc](https://giong.run/docs/giong-grpc.md) |
| PostgreSQL | sqlx, tokio-postgres | [giong-postgres](https://giong.run/docs/giong-postgres.md) |
| MySQL | sqlx | [giong-mysql](https://giong.run/docs/giong-mysql.md) |
| Redis | redis-rs | [giong-redis](https://giong.run/docs/giong-redis.md) |

Crates that need no runtime (serde, rustls, Tokio's `sync`) work as they are. For a protocol giong has no crate for, such as WebSocket, a crate generic over a Tokio or futures-io stream runs through [giong-compat](https://giong.run/docs/giong-compat.md) (`giong_compat::Compat::new(stream)`), at the cost of a copy per byte. Crates that need the Tokio runtime itself (sqlx, reqwest, tonic's transport, most cloud SDKs) panic on a giong worker with "there is no reactor running".

## Let the tools find the rest

`giong check` reports the mistakes a port usually leaves: a blocking call inside async code (`GIONG-E5006`), a listener bound to a host name (`GIONG-E5007`), a `RefCell` borrow held across an `.await` (`GIONG-E5008`). `giong doctor` lists dependencies that need the Tokio runtime.

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md -->

# Deploying giong

giong is fastest on io_uring, which needs Linux 6.0 or newer (6.1 or newer recommended)
and the three io_uring system calls: `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter` and
`io_uring_register`. Many container platforms block them by default.

Where io_uring cannot be used, giong runs on its **epoll driver** instead, without being
told: in a Docker container with the default seccomp profile, in Kubernetes with the
`RuntimeDefault` profile, under gVisor, with the `kernel.io_uring_disabled` sysctl set,
on a kernel older than 6.0, or on Linux 6.14 to 7.2 when the
[locked-memory limit](#locked-memory-limit) is used up. Every API works the same way on
both drivers; epoll makes more system calls per request, and file operations run on a
pool of blocking threads.
When giong falls back by itself it says so once on stderr, with the reason (the same
`GIONG-E…` error a runtime that insists on io_uring would get). `giong::driver_choice()`
tells which driver a worker got, who chose it, and why io_uring is not used; log it at
startup:

```rust
giong::block_on(async {
    eprintln!("giong driver: {}", giong::driver_choice());
    // io_uring (chosen automatically)
});
```

`giong-mcp`'s `overview` shows the same for each worker. The
[benchmarks](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/BENCHMARKS.md#io_uring-against-epoll) have the measured difference.

So a container needs no special settings to run giong. Allow io_uring, as this page shows,
when you want its speed:

- `Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring` in the environment,
  makes the runtime fail to start where io_uring is blocked, instead of running on epoll.
  The error begins with `giong needs io_uring, which is not available here`
  ([GIONG-E0001](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E0001.md)).
- `Builder::driver(DriverKind::Epoll)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=epoll`, uses epoll even where
  io_uring is available.

## Check a machine

```sh
uname -r                              # 6.0 or newer
cat /proc/sys/kernel/io_uring_disabled  # Linux 6.6+: 0 = allowed
ulimit -l                             # Linux 6.14-7.2: unlimited, or 150 KiB per worker
```

`kernel.io_uring_disabled` (Linux 6.6 and newer): `0` allows io_uring for every process,
`1` only for privileged processes and members of the group in `kernel.io_uring_group`,
`2` for nobody. Set it with `sysctl -w kernel.io_uring_disabled=0`, or put the service's
user in that group.

## Locked-memory limit

Linux 6.14 to 7.2 count the memory of every io_uring ring against the locked-memory limit
(`RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, `ulimit -l`) of a process that lacks `CAP_IPC_LOCK`. Linux 7.3 stopped,
and so did 6.18 from 6.18.58; distribution kernels may have taken the change too. The
count is kept per user ID and summed over all of that user's processes, and the memory of
a closed ring is given back a moment after the close. A giong worker locks about 150 KiB
with the default settings: the submission and completion queues take 136 KiB of it
(`Builder::ring_entries`), the two rings of receive buffers 8 KiB each
(`Builder::recv_buffers`). The usual default limit of 8 MiB holds about fifty workers, for
all of the user's processes together; the 64 KiB of older systems holds none.

A worker that cannot lock the memory gets `ENOMEM` from the kernel, which giong reports as
[GIONG-E0010](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E0010.md), naming the limit; without an explicit driver it runs that
worker on epoll and says so once on stderr. Root is not held to the limit, since it has
`CAP_IPC_LOCK`, except where that capability was taken away, as in a Docker container.
Raise the limit, or lift it, for any service that is not root:

- systemd: `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` in the `[Service]` section, or
  `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_IPC_LOCK` to lift it for a service with a `User=`.
- Docker: `docker run --ulimit memlock=-1:-1`, or in Docker Compose:

  ```yaml
  services:
    api:
      ulimits:
        memlock:
          soft: -1
          hard: -1
  ```

- Kubernetes has no setting for the limit. Add the capability where the pod's security
  policy allows it (`securityContext.capabilities.add: ["IPC_LOCK"]`; Pod Security's
  `baseline` and `restricted` levels do not), or raise the limit the container runtime
  starts containers with on each node (for containerd, `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` in a
  drop-in for its systemd unit). Containers that run as the same user ID on one node share
  the count.
- A shell: `ulimit -l unlimited` as root before starting the service, or an entry in
  `/etc/security/limits.conf` for its user.

Or need less: fewer workers, a smaller `Builder::ring_entries`, fewer receive buffers. Or
run a kernel that does not count the rings.

## Ubuntu 24.04

Ubuntu's 6.8 kernels from 6.8.0-135 on have a bug that makes them refuse every correctly
formed io_uring buffer ring, which giong's io_uring driver needs: a backport inverted a
check on the request's reserved fields. The AWS, Azure, GCP and Oracle 6.8 kernels built
from them have it too, as does the 6.8 HWE kernel of Ubuntu 22.04. giong recognises the bug and registers its ring
the way those kernels accept, so io_uring works there at full speed, and
`giong::driver_choice()` lists the workaround (`buffer-ring-reserved-check`). Nothing to
do on your side. Other software that uses buffer rings through liburing fails on those
kernels with `EINVAL`. The 7.0 HWE kernel (`linux-generic-hwe-24.04`) does not have the
bug.

## Linux 6.0.16 to 6.0.19

The last four releases of the 6.0 series (which is no longer maintained) return 1
instead of -1 from bind(2) on a TCP socket whose address is in use, and leave the socket
unbound. Programs read that as success, and listen(2) then puts the socket on a free port
of every interface, so a server asked for a busy port starts on another one.
`giong::net::TcpListener::bind` checks which port the socket ended up on and fails with
`AddrInUse`, as on every other kernel. A listener that the standard library bound, handed
over with `TcpListener::from_std`, is not checked: compare its `local_addr()` with the
address you asked for, or let giong bind it. 6.0.15 and older, 6.1 and later, and UDP and
Unix sockets are not affected.

## Restarting on the same port

`TcpListener::bind`, `bind_balanced` and `UdpSocket::bind` let the workers of one process
share a port, and refuse it, with `AddrInUse`, while a socket of another process holds
it: a service started twice by mistake fails the second time instead of quietly taking
half of the first one's connections. What that means for a restart:

- Stopping the old process before starting the new one (systemd's `Restart=`, a container
  replaced by its orchestrator) needs nothing: the port of a closed listener can be bound
  again at once.
- Starting the new version on the same machine and port while the old one still serves
  fails until the old one has let the port go. Run the two on different ports behind the
  load balancer or proxy, or create the sockets outside giong: one per worker, with
  `SO_REUSEPORT` set (with the `socket2` crate, say) by every process that is to share the
  port, wrapped with `TcpListener::from_std` or `UdpSocket::from_std` in each worker.
  giong sets no option on such a socket and does not check who else holds its port.
- Connections still in a closing listener's accept queue are refused when it closes: have
  the load balancer stop sending to the old process first, and give it a
  `Builder::shutdown_grace` to answer what it already has.

## Sizing memory

What a giong-http server holds is bounded by its settings, per worker (each worker runs its
own `serve`):

```text
memory per worker  ≈  max_buffered_request_bytes
                    + open connections × (idle cost + up to 4 KiB while a request arrives)
                    + what the handlers hold
```

- `max_buffered_request_bytes` bounds the requests the worker is receiving in full: by
  default 64 MiB, or a quarter of the cgroup memory limit divided among the workers if that
  is less, so that one worker in a 128 MiB container takes 32 MiB at most. Past it, requests
  are refused with `503` (HTTP/1.1) or `REFUSED_STREAM` (HTTP/2) instead of being buffered
  ([GIONG-E1120](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E1120.md)). Bodies read as a stream (`Handler::stream_body`) hold
  one piece at a time and are not counted.
- An idle connection costs about 2 KiB over HTTP/1.1, 4.5 KiB over HTTP/2 and 10.5 KiB over
  HTTPS in the process, and the kernel about 4 KiB more per socket (charged to the
  container's memory under cgroup v2). `max_connections` (10,000 per `serve` call by
  default) bounds the count.

The defaults fit the budget to the container, but not the number of connections: 10,000
idle HTTPS connections take about 145 MiB with the kernel's share. Past what fits, the
server does not get killed: while less than `min_free_memory` is left to the process (a
tenth of the container's limit by default, between 16 and 256 MiB), it refuses new
connections with `503` and `Retry-After: 1`, or closes them before the TLS handshake
([GIONG-E1121](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E1121.md)), and keeps serving the ones it holds. That is a last line
of defence, which refuses clients the load balancer could have sent elsewhere. In a small
container, lower `max_connections` to what fits next to the budget, so that the server
stops accepting before memory runs low:

```rust
use giong_http::Server;

// One worker in a 256 MiB container, serving HTTPS: 64 MiB for requests being
// received, 5,000 connections x ~17 KiB = 83 MiB, and the rest for the program.
let server = Server::new()
    .max_buffered_request_bytes(64 << 20)
    .max_connections(5_000);
```

CI checks the bound: the `slow-uploads` job runs a server with one worker and with four in
a Docker container limited to 128 MiB, sends it hundreds of uploads that stop one byte short
of their announced length, over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, and fails if the container is
OOM-killed or a well-behaved client mixed in stops getting answers
([scripts/slow-uploads.sh](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/scripts/slow-uploads.sh)). The same job then runs it in 48 MiB
and opens idle connections until it refuses them, and fails if the container is
OOM-killed, if the connections it holds stop being served, or if it does not take new ones
once those close ([scripts/idle-connections.sh](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/scripts/idle-connections.sh)).

## Docker

Docker's default seccomp profile does not allow the io_uring system calls, so in a
container run with default settings giong uses its epoll driver. For io_uring, use a
profile that is Docker's default plus those three calls:

```sh
curl -fsSLo docker-default.json \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/profiles/main/seccomp/default.json
jq '.syscalls += [{"names": ["io_uring_setup", "io_uring_enter", "io_uring_register"],
                   "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"}]' docker-default.json > giong-seccomp.json

docker run --security-opt seccomp=giong-seccomp.json your-image
```

With Docker Compose:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: your-image
    security_opt:
      - seccomp=giong-seccomp.json
```

This keeps every other restriction of the default profile. Avoid
`--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`, which turns all of them off.

Checked on Docker Engine 29.9.2 with a static binary that starts a runtime and does a TCP
round trip: with `giong-seccomp.json` it runs on io_uring. With the default profile,
giong's test suite runs on the epoll driver in CI (the `docker` job).

## Kubernetes

A pod's containers get the container runtime's default profile when their
`securityContext.seccompProfile.type` is `RuntimeDefault`, and also by default on
kubelets started with `--seccomp-default`. Pod Security's `restricted` level requires
either `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost`. containerd's default profile blocks io_uring like Docker's does.

Install `giong-seccomp.json` from above on every node, under the kubelet's seccomp
directory (by default `/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/`), for example as
`profiles/giong.json`, and point the container at it:

```yaml
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: Localhost
    localhostProfile: profiles/giong.json
```

The [Security Profiles Operator](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/security-profiles-operator)
can distribute the profile to the nodes for you. Managed platforms differ in what they
let you change; check that yours allows `Localhost` profiles.

## CPU limits

giong starts one worker per CPU the process may use: the CPUs it may run on (`--cpuset-cpus`,
the exclusive CPUs of Kubernetes' static CPU manager), fewer when a CPU quota allows less
(`--cpus`, `resources.limits.cpu`), rounded down, and at least one. A pod limited to 2 CPUs
on a 64-core node gets 2 workers. Tokio and `std::thread::available_parallelism` count the
same way.

A fraction is rounded down on purpose. Measured with the `defaults` example, wrk with 64
connections, io_uring ([raw data](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/bench/results/containers/cpu-quota.txt)):

| Quota | Workers | Requests/s | p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 CPUs | 2 (default) | 285k | 0.55 ms |
| 2 CPUs | 4 | 248k | 4.1 ms |
| 1.5 CPUs | 1 (default) | 147k | 1.0-2.0 ms |
| 1.5 CPUs | 2 | 214k | 23 ms |
| 0.5 CPUs | 1 (default) | 70k | 50 ms |

More workers than the quota run until the quota is used up and then wait for the next
100 ms period: more requests per second, and a p99 10 to 20 times higher. Set
`Builder::workers` above the default only when throughput matters more than tail latency.
Under one CPU, the 100 ms period itself sets the p99 near 50 ms whatever the program does;
give a latency-sensitive service at least one whole CPU.

Kubernetes CPU requests without a limit set no quota: the process sees every CPU of the node,
and giong starts a worker for each. That costs little memory (about 0.4 MiB per worker under
load, [raw data](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/bench/results/containers/memory-workers.txt)), but the workers share the
CPU time the pod gets. Pass the request to the program and use it, for example:

```yaml
env:
  - name: WORKERS
    valueFrom:
      resourceFieldRef:
        resource: requests.cpu   # whole CPUs, rounded up
```

```rust
let mut builder = giong::Builder::new();
if let Some(n) = std::env::var("WORKERS").ok().and_then(|n| n.parse().ok()) {
    builder = builder.workers(n);
}
```

## Thread and file limits

Each worker is a thread, and so is each of up to 64 threads that run file operations on the
epoll driver. A container's PID limit counts threads (`docker run --pids-limit`, the
kubelet's `podPidsLimit`, `TasksMax` in systemd): when it is reached, `Runtime::run`
returns [GIONG-E0020](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E0020.md), which names the worker that could not start and the
container's `pids.max`. Allow at least the workers, your own threads and 64 more.

Each connection is a file descriptor, and the soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` (`ulimit -n`) bounds
them. containerd from 1.8 on, and so Kubernetes on most nodes today, starts containers with
the systemd default of 1,024 soft and 524,288 hard. At the soft limit giong-http's accept loop
waits 50 ms and tries again, serving the connections it has, while new clients wait in the
listen queue: measured with the `defaults` example in a container limited to 1,024 files,
1,071 of 1,100 keep-alive clients were answered and 29 were not.

So on Linux giong raises the soft limit to the hard one when a runtime is built, as Go
programs do: a process may do that without privileges, and with it all 1,100 clients are
answered in the same container. A hard limit of `unlimited` is read as `fs.nr_open`. To
keep the soft limit, for a program that starts children which still use `select(2)` and
need descriptors below 1,024 (children inherit the limit), build with
`Builder::raise_open_files_limit(false)`. A hard limit below what the service needs is
raised from outside: `docker run --ulimit nofile=65536:65536`, `ulimits` in Compose,
`LimitNOFILE` in systemd. When a server does run out, each worker says so on stderr at most
once a minute, with the limits it found ([GIONG-E1123](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E1123.md)), and giong-mcp's
`overview` shows the limits of the container (CPUs, CPU quota, memory, `pids.max`, open
files) beside where the worker count came from.

## Stopping: SIGTERM and process 1

`docker stop` and Kubernetes send `SIGTERM`, then `SIGKILL` 10 seconds later (Kubernetes:
`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, 30 by default). A program that runs as process 1 of a
container gets no default action for `SIGTERM`: unless it handles the signal, it keeps
running until it is killed. With `Builder::shutdown_on_signals(true)` giong handles
`SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`, and with `shutdown_grace` the requests in flight are answered first;
the `rest-api` example stops in under half a second. Without it, run the container with
`--init` (`init: true` in Docker Compose), which forwards the signal and stops the process.

## Container image

[examples/rest-api/Dockerfile](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/examples/rest-api/Dockerfile) builds the `rest-api` example
into a 44 MB image (distroless, glibc, no shell, an unprivileged user), and
[compose.yaml](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/examples/rest-api/compose.yaml) runs it with PostgreSQL and Redis, a CPU
and a memory limit, and the lines that allow io_uring. Copy them for a service of your own:
giong needs nothing in the image besides the program.

## Sandboxes

Runtimes that put a user-space kernel between the container and Linux, such as gVisor
(used by GKE Sandbox), do not offer io_uring by default. giong runs on epoll there; run it
outside such a sandbox for io_uring. gVisor's optional io_uring (`runsc --iouring`) takes
none of the settings giong's rings need, so giong runs on epoll there too, with
[GIONG-E0001](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E0001.md) as the reason.

gVisor's network stack decides whether sockets may share a port when each one binds,
where Linux decides when the next one binds. giong finds out once per process which way
the system works, and its workers share a port either way. CI runs the tests that bind
one port from several workers, and a four-worker server, under gVisor
([scripts/gvisor.sh](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/scripts/gvisor.sh)).

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/README.md -->

# Error codes

Every error giong raises itself starts with a code and ends with a link to its page here:

```text
GIONG-E0102: no address found for db.internal. Fix: check the spelling of the name,
/etc/hosts, and the DNS servers in /etc/resolv.conf (in a container, the network it is
attached to). See https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/main/docs/errors/E0102.md
```

Errors giong only passes on, such as "connection refused" from the kernel, have no code.
Functions still return `std::io::Error`; match on the code, not on the message:

```rust
use giong::error::{self, Code};

fn on_error(err: &std::io::Error) {
    if error::code(err) == Some(Code::HostNotFound) {
        // ...
    }
}
```

giong-http, giong-web, giong-tls, giong-postgres, giong-mysql, giong-redis, giong-mcp and
giong-compat use the same codes. A code is never reused or renumbered, and its page stays
when it is no longer raised.

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0001.md -->

# GIONG-E0001: io_uring is not available

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::IoUringUnavailable`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), and `io_uring_setup` failed with `EPERM`, `EACCES` or `ENOSYS`, or with `EINVAL` for a ring Linux sets up from 5.6 on. The kernel has io_uring but this process may not use it, the kernel (or a sandbox in front of it) does not have it at all, or the sandbox has only part of it (gVisor with `runsc --iouring` takes no setup flags). Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver instead. The error keeps the kernel's `io::ErrorKind` (`PermissionDenied`, `Unsupported` or `InvalidInput`), and the kernel's error is its `source()`.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`, and giong falls back to epoll by itself.
- In Docker, the default seccomp profile blocks io_uring. Run with a profile that allows `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter` and `io_uring_register` (see [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://giong.run/docs/deployment.md)), or `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` to confirm that this is the cause.
- In Kubernetes, the container runtime applies the same default profile: set a `seccompProfile` of type `Localhost` that allows the three calls, as [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://giong.run/docs/deployment.md) shows.
- On the host, `sysctl kernel.io_uring_disabled` must be `0`, or `1` with the process in the group named by `kernel.io_uring_group`.
- gVisor and some other sandboxes do not offer io_uring by default, and gVisor's optional one (`runsc --iouring`) is too small for giong; run giong outside them, or on its epoll driver.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0002.md -->

# GIONG-E0002: the kernel is too old

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::KernelTooOld`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), and the kernel is missing an io_uring feature giong needs: registering a ring of receive buffers (`IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING`) failed. It arrived in Linux 5.19 and works reliably from 6.0, the oldest kernel giong's io_uring driver supports. Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver, which works on older kernels.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`.
- Run on Linux 6.0 or newer; 6.1 or newer is faster (giong then uses `IORING_SETUP_DEFER_TASKRUN`). `uname -r` shows the version.
- On a managed platform, pick a node image with a newer kernel.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0003.md -->

# GIONG-E0003: another runtime handles the signals

Raised by the runtime, when it starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::SignalsTaken`.

## What happened

The runtime was built with `Builder::shutdown_on_signals(true)`, but another giong runtime in this process already handles `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`. Signal handlers belong to the whole process, so only one runtime at a time can own them.

## How to fix it

- Turn on `shutdown_on_signals` for one runtime only, and stop the others through their `Handle::shutdown`.
- Or run one runtime at a time: the handlers are released when that runtime's `run` returns.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0004.md -->

# GIONG-E0004: invalid runtime setting

Raised by the runtime, when it starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::InvalidConfig`.

## What happened

A runtime setting is outside the range giong accepts, such as the number or the size of the receive buffers, or the `GIONG_DRIVER` environment variable names no driver.

## How to fix it

- Read the message: it names the setting, the range and the value given.
- `Builder::recv_buffers(count, size)` takes up to 32768 buffers, rounded up to a power of two, and a size from 64 bytes to 4 GiB.
- `GIONG_DRIVER` takes `io_uring` or `epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on macOS and `iocp` on Windows; unset or empty (or `auto`) means io_uring where the kernel allows it and epoll elsewhere on Linux, kqueue on macOS and iocp on Windows. It is read only when the code does not call `Builder::driver`. A driver the operating system does not have is refused with this code too (io_uring with `GIONG-E0001`).

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0005.md -->

# GIONG-E0005: unexpected result from the kernel

Raised by the runtime's I/O operations, and as a panic that stops the worker when its event loop gets an error it cannot go on after (from `io_uring_enter` or `epoll_wait`). In code: `giong::error::Code::Unexpected`.

## What happened

The kernel returned something giong does not expect, such as received data without a buffer or a datagram from an unknown address family. It points to a bug in giong or in the kernel, with one exception: a panic naming `EBADR` or `ENOMEM` means the kernel ran out of memory and dropped completions, after which the worker cannot know which operations finished.

## How to fix it

- If the message names `EBADR` or `ENOMEM`: give the process more memory, or run fewer connections per worker.
- Otherwise, please report it at https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/issues with the message, your kernel version (`uname -r`) and, if you can, a way to reproduce it.
- Running the same program on another kernel version helps tell the two apart.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0006.md -->

# GIONG-E0006: read used after recv

Raised by `TcpStream`, `UnixStream` and `UdpSocket`. In code: `giong::error::Code::MixedReads`.

## What happened

A one-off read (`read`, `read_from`) was used on a stream or socket that already has a multishot receive (`recv`, `recv_from`) running. The kernel keeps delivering data into the multishot receive, so a one-off read would see the data out of order.

On a `UnixStream`, `recv_with_fds` counts as a one-off read: it cannot follow `recv`, and once it has been used, `recv` is refused, because a multishot receive would let the kernel close descriptors that arrive.

## How to fix it

- Use one way of reading per stream or socket: `recv`/`recv_from` (buffers from the runtime's pool, best for many connections) or `read`/`read_from` (your own buffer).

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0007.md -->

# GIONG-E0007: the time limit passed

Raised by `giong::time::timeout`, when its error becomes an `io::Error`. In code: `giong::error::Code::TimedOut`.

## What happened

The future given to `giong::time::timeout` did not finish within its time limit, and the `Elapsed` error was turned into an `io::Error` (by `?` in a function returning `io::Result`). The future was dropped, which cancels its I/O.

## How to fix it

- Give it more time if the limit is too tight for the work.
- Otherwise find out why the operation is slow: the peer, the network, or a task that keeps the worker busy (one worker runs every task on its core).

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0008.md -->

# GIONG-E0008: no such worker

Raised by `giong::Handle::spawn_on`, as a panic. In code: `giong::error::Code::NoSuchWorker`.

## What happened

`spawn_on` was given a worker index that the runtime does not have. Workers are numbered from 0 to `Handle::workers() - 1`. This is a bug in the calling code, so `spawn_on` panics instead of returning an error.

## How to fix it

- Pass an index below `Handle::workers()`. To spread work over every worker, use `i % handle.workers()`.
- `Builder::workers` sets the count; without it, the runtime starts one worker for each CPU the process may run on, which differs between machines and containers.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0009.md -->

# GIONG-E0009: the kernel refused io_uring buffer rings

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::BufferRingRefused`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), the kernel is 6.0 or newer, and it would not register giong's ring of receive buffers (`IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING`). Such a kernel should accept it, and giong already works around the kernel bugs it knows here, such as the inverted check in Ubuntu's 6.8.0-135 and later kernels (`giong::KernelWorkaround`). The message names the kernel release, the kernel's error is the `source()`, and its `io::ErrorKind` is kept. Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`. `giong::driver_choice()` then reports this same error as the reason giong chose epoll.
- `ENOMEM` means the memory for the ring could not be had: check the service's memory cgroup limit, or give it fewer receive buffers (`Builder::recv_buffers`). When the locked-memory limit is the cause (Linux 6.14 to 7.2 count buffer rings against it), giong raises [GIONG-E0010](https://giong.run/docs/errors/E0010.md) instead.
- `EINVAL` on a 6.x kernel is most likely a kernel bug giong does not know yet. Please report it with the output of `uname -r` at <https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/issues>; a newer kernel of the same distribution may already have it fixed.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0010.md -->

# GIONG-E0010: the locked-memory limit is used up

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::LockedMemoryLimit`.

## What happened

Setting up the worker's io_uring failed with `ENOMEM`, and the process is held to a locked-memory limit (`RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, `ulimit -l`): it is not unlimited, and the process lacks `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, which would lift it. Linux 6.14 to 7.2 count the memory of every io_uring ring against that limit: the submission and completion queues, and each buffer ring (7.3 stopped, and so did 6.18 from 6.18.58). The count is kept per user ID, summed over all of that user's processes, and the kernel gives the memory of a closed ring back a moment after the close, not at once. A giong worker locks about 150 KiB with the default settings, so a limit of 8 MiB, a common default, holds about fifty workers, and one of 64 KiB, the default on older systems, holds none. The message names the limit and what the memory was for ("rings" or "buffer ring"); the kernel's error is the `source()`, and its `io::ErrorKind` (`OutOfMemory`) is kept.

Without `Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`, giong runs such a worker on its epoll driver instead, says so once on stderr, and `giong::driver_choice()` reports this error as the reason. Workers that got their rings before the limit was used up stay on io_uring.

## How to fix it

- Raise the limit for the service: `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` in its systemd unit, `--ulimit memlock=-1` with `docker run` (in Docker Compose, `memlock` under `ulimits` with `soft: -1` and `hard: -1`), or `ulimit -l unlimited` in the shell that starts it. [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md#locked-memory-limit) has the details, Kubernetes included.
- Or give the process `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, which lifts the limit (`AmbientCapabilities=CAP_IPC_LOCK` in a systemd unit, `--cap-add IPC_LOCK` with `docker run`).
- Or need less: fewer workers (`Builder::workers`), smaller rings (`Builder::ring_entries`), fewer receive buffers (`Builder::recv_buffers`). Other processes of the same user ID count too, other containers running as that ID on the same machine included.
- Or run a kernel that does not count io_uring's rings: Linux 7.3 or newer, or 6.18.58 or newer in the 6.18 series.
- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0011.md -->

# GIONG-E0011: not inside a giong runtime

Raised by everything that needs a giong worker, as a panic: `giong::spawn`, `giong::time::sleep` and `timeout` when polled, `giong::handle`, `giong::worker_id`, `TcpStream::connect`, `TcpListener::bind`, the file operations, and the rest of the I/O API. In code: `giong::error::Code::NotInRuntime`.

## What happened

The call ran on a thread where no giong runtime runs: a plain thread, a thread of another runtime such as Tokio's, or a `Drop` that ran after the runtime had stopped. giong's I/O and timers live on the worker thread that uses them (each worker has its own io_uring or epoll instance), so they cannot work without one. This is a bug in the calling code, so giong panics instead of returning an error.

## How to fix it

- Start a runtime and call the function from the futures it runs: `giong::block_on(async { ... })` for one thread, or `giong::Builder::new().build()?.run(|worker| async move { ... })` for one worker per CPU.
- Do not await giong futures on another executor (`tokio::spawn`, `futures::executor::block_on`, an async test macro other than giong's). To use giong's sockets with crates written for Tokio's or futures' I/O traits, wrap them with `giong-compat` inside a giong runtime; it adapts the I/O traits, not the runtime.
- From another thread, send work to the runtime with a `giong::Handle` (from `Runtime::handle` or `giong::handle()`): `Handle::spawn_on` or `Handle::spawn_balanced`, whose handles can be awaited from any thread.
- Library code that may run inside or outside giong can check `giong::try_worker_id()`, which returns `None` outside a runtime.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0012.md -->

# GIONG-E0012: a runtime already runs on this thread

Raised by `giong::block_on` and `giong::Builder::block_on`, as a panic. In code: `giong::error::Code::RuntimeAlreadyRunning`.

## What happened

`block_on` was called on a thread where a giong runtime is already running, usually from inside a task or a main future. One thread runs at most one giong worker, and a nested `block_on` would stop every other task of that worker until it returned. This is a bug in the calling code, so giong panics instead of returning an error.

## How to fix it

- Inside a giong task, `.await` the future instead of calling `block_on` on it.
- To run work next to the current task, use `giong::spawn`; to run it on another worker, `Handle::spawn_on` or `Handle::spawn_balanced`, and await the handle they return.
- If a separate runtime is really wanted (for example a test that starts its own), start it on a thread of its own: `std::thread::spawn(|| giong::block_on(...))`.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0013.md -->

# GIONG-E0013: an operation was polled on another worker

Raised by giong's I/O futures, as a panic. In code: `giong::error::Code::WrongWorker`.

## What happened

A future that had started an I/O operation (a read, a write, a connect, a file operation) on one giong worker was polled again on a different worker or runtime. The operation lives in the first worker's io_uring or epoll instance, and only that worker can collect its result. giong's futures are not `Send`, so this takes unusual code: a future kept from one `block_on` and polled in the next one, or a future moved between threads with `unsafe`. This is a bug in the calling code, so giong panics instead of returning an error.

## How to fix it

- Await a giong future to completion on the worker that first polled it, within the same `block_on` or `Runtime::run`.
- Send data between workers and threads, not futures: `Handle::spawn_on` takes a closure and builds the future on the worker that runs it, and channels (`giong::sync`) carry values.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0014.md -->

# GIONG-E0014: the compute lane is full

Raised by `giong::try_spawn_compute` and `Handle::try_spawn_compute`. In code: `giong::error::Code::ComputeBusy`. Its `io::ErrorKind` is `WouldBlock`.

## What happened

Every thread of the compute lane was busy and as many closures as `Builder::compute_backlog` allows (by default four per compute thread) were already waiting for one. The new closure was dropped without running. `giong::spawn_compute`, which never refuses, would have queued it behind the others.

## How to fix it

- Under overload this is the intended answer: shed the request (an HTTP server answers 503 with `Retry-After`) instead of queueing work that will finish too late to matter.
- If the lane is behind all the time, the machine needs more CPU for this work: give it more compute threads (`Builder::compute_threads`), fewer workers so those threads get CPUs of their own, or make each job cheaper.
- If short bursts are refused while the average load is fine, raise `Builder::compute_backlog` so a burst can wait.
- `Handle::lane_stats()` shows the compute lane's busy threads and queued closures.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0016.md -->

# GIONG-E0016: this signal cannot be listened for

Raised by `giong::signal::listen`. In code: `giong::error::Code::SignalNotAllowed`.

## What happened

`listen` was given a signal that a program cannot, or should not, receive as a stream:

- `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP`: the kernel never lets a process catch them.
- `SIGSEGV`, `SIGBUS`, `SIGILL` and `SIGFPE`: they report a fault in the program itself (a bad memory access, an illegal instruction). Handling them later, on a worker, would let the faulting code run on.
- A number that is not a signal: 0, negative, or above `SIGRTMAX`.

## How to fix it

- Listen for the signals meant for programs to act on: `SignalKind::HANGUP` (reload the configuration), `SignalKind::USER1`/`USER2` (your own actions, such as a dump), `SignalKind::INTERRUPT`/`TERMINATE` (stop), `SignalKind::CHILD`, `SignalKind::WINDOW_CHANGE`, or a real-time signal from `SignalKind::from_raw(libc::SIGRTMIN() + n)`.
- To stop on `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`, `Builder::shutdown_on_signals(true)` with `giong::shutdown_signal()` is usually all you need.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0017.md -->

# GIONG-E0017: descriptors could not be passed

Raised by `send_with_fds`, `send_to_with_fds` and `recv_with_fds` of `giong::net::UnixStream` and `giong::net::UnixDatagram`. In code: `giong::error::Code::FdPassing`.

## What happened

One of these:

- **More than 253 descriptors for one message.** Linux passes at most 253 (`SCM_MAX_FD`, `giong::net::MAX_FDS`) per `sendmsg`. Nothing was sent.
- **Descriptors with an empty buffer.** Descriptors travel with the bytes of a message, and a stream socket sends nothing at all for an empty send, so they would be lost. Nothing was sent.
- **The kernel cut off the control data of a received message** (`MSG_CTRUNC`). The descriptors that did not fit were closed by the kernel before they arrived, and giong closed the ones that did, so the message is incomplete. giong leaves room for 253 descriptors and for credentials, so this happens only when the sender attached other control data as well, or the socket has options such as `SO_PASSCRED` turned on.

## How to fix it

- Send at most 253 descriptors per call; split a larger set over several messages.
- Send at least one byte with the descriptors, such as a message that says what they are.
- On a socket that receives descriptors, turn off other control data (`SO_PASSCRED`, `SO_TIMESTAMP` and similar), and have the sender attach only `SCM_RIGHTS`.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0018.md -->

# GIONG-E0018: the inherited socket cannot be used that way

Raised by `giong::net::activated_sockets` and the methods of `giong::net::ActivatedSocket`. In code: `giong::error::Code::ActivatedSocket`.

## What happened

One of these:

- **The sockets were already taken.** systemd (or another socket manager speaking its protocol) hands a service its sockets as descriptors 3, 4, ... and says so in `LISTEN_FDS` and `LISTEN_PID`. `activated_sockets` takes ownership of them, so a second call would hand out the same descriptors twice; it fails instead.
- **The socket is not the kind asked for.** `tcp_listener` was called on a socket that is not a listening TCP socket (a UDP socket, a Unix socket, a TCP socket that is not listening), and likewise `unix_listener`, `udp_socket` and `unix_datagram`. The message says what the socket is.

## How to fix it

- Call `activated_sockets` once, early in `main`, and share the result (an `Arc<Vec<ActivatedSocket>>`) with the workers. Each worker then calls `tcp_listener()` (or the method for its kind) on the socket, which gives it its own descriptor.
- Match the method to the socket in the `.socket` unit: `ListenStream=` with an address or port is a TCP listener, `ListenStream=` with a path a Unix listener, `ListenDatagram=` with a port a UDP socket, with a path a Unix datagram socket. `FileDescriptorName=` names a socket, and `ActivatedSocket::name` returns that name, so pick sockets by name rather than by position.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0019.md -->

# GIONG-E0019: cannot watch the child process

Raised by `giong::process::Command::spawn` and the methods of `giong::process::Child`. In code: `giong::error::Code::ChildProcess`.

## What happened

giong waits for a child process through a pidfd, a descriptor for the process that the kernel makes readable when it exits, so that waiting needs no thread and no `SIGCHLD` handler, and a signal can never reach another process that got the same process ID later. One of these went wrong:

- **The kernel refused the pidfd** (`pidfd_open`): Linux older than 5.3, or a seccomp profile that blocks the call. The child was started; giong killed and reaped it, since it could not have waited for it.
- **Someone else reaped the child.** Code in the same process called `waitpid(-1, ...)` or `wait()`, or set `SIGCHLD` to `SIG_IGN`, which makes the kernel reap children by itself. The exit status is gone.

## How to fix it

- Run on Linux 5.3 or newer, and allow `pidfd_open` and `pidfd_send_signal` in the seccomp profile (Docker's default profile allows both since Docker 20.10).
- Do not reap children that giong started: no `waitpid(-1, ...)`, no `wait()`, no `SIGCHLD` set to `SIG_IGN`, in your code or in a library you call. Listening for `SIGCHLD` with `giong::signal::listen` is fine: it does not reap.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0020.md -->

# GIONG-E0020: a worker thread could not be started

Raised by the runtime, by `Runtime::run`. In code: `giong::error::Code::ThreadLimit`.

## What happened

giong runs each worker on a thread of its own, and starting one of them failed. The kernel says only `EAGAIN` ("Resource temporarily unavailable"), which nearly always means the process may not have more threads: every thread counts as a task against the PID limit of the process's cgroup (`pids.max`), and against `RLIMIT_NPROC` (`ulimit -u`), which is summed over all processes of the same user. Containers often set the first: `docker run --pids-limit`, the PID limit of a Kubernetes pod (`podPidsLimit` in the kubelet's settings), `TasksMax` in a systemd unit, and sandboxes that run code for AI agents. The message says which worker could not start and, where it can be read, the container's `pids.max`; the kernel's error is the `source()`, and its `io::ErrorKind` (`WouldBlock`) is kept.

The workers that had started are stopped again, and `run` returns this error; nothing has run.

## How to fix it

- Raise the limit: `--pids-limit` with `docker run` (`pids_limit` in Docker Compose), the kubelet's `podPidsLimit`, `TasksMax=` in the systemd unit, or `ulimit -u` in the shell that starts the service. Count one thread per worker, the program's own threads, and on the epoll driver up to 64 more for file operations.
- Or start fewer workers: `Builder::workers`. By default giong starts one per CPU the process may use, which on a large machine without a CPU limit can be more than a small PID limit allows.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0080.md -->

# GIONG-E0080: the budget is at its limit

Raised by `Budget::try_spawn`, `Budget::try_reserve` and `Budget::try_spawn_compute` in `giong::budget`, and by `giong::try_spawn_compute` inside a task of a budget. In code: `giong::error::Code::BudgetFull`. Its `io::ErrorKind` is `WouldBlock`.

## What happened

The budget (one tenant's share of the runtime) already holds as much as one of its `Limits` allows: tasks alive, bytes reserved, or compute closures queued and running; or other calls already wait for room in it. The message names the budget, the limit, what is in use and how many wait. The work was dropped without running. The waiting forms (`Budget::spawn`, `Budget::reserve`, `Budget::spawn_compute`) would have waited their turn instead.

## How to fix it

- Under overload this is the intended answer: the tenant has as much in progress as it may, so shed the request (an HTTP server answers 503 with `Retry-After`) rather than queue work for it. Other tenants are not affected.
- If the tenant's normal load needs more, raise its limits with `Budget::set_limits`.
- To wait for room instead of refusing, use the waiting form of the call, bounded with `giong::time::timeout`.
- `Budget::stats()` shows what each resource of the budget holds, its peak, and how many calls waited or were refused.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0081.md -->

# GIONG-E0081: a reservation larger than the budget

Raised by `Budget::reserve` and `Budget::try_reserve` in `giong::budget`. In code: `giong::error::Code::BudgetTooSmall`. Its `io::ErrorKind` is `InvalidInput`.

## What happened

The reservation asked for more bytes than the budget's whole memory limit (`Limits::memory`). It could never be granted, however long it waited, so it failed at once instead of waiting forever.

## How to fix it

- Raise the budget's memory limit above the largest reservation its work makes (`Budget::set_limits`).
- Or reserve in parts: a request body can be reserved as it arrives, in chunks, with each chunk's reservation kept until the body is dropped.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0028.md -->

# GIONG-E0028: the system ran out of network buffers

Raised by `TcpStream` and `UnixStream` writes and connects (giong-tls streams included) on macOS. In code: `giong::error::Code::NetworkBuffersExhausted`. The error kind is `OutOfMemory`, and the kernel's `ENOBUFS` is the `source()`, so `raw_os_error()` stays reachable.

## What happened

When macOS has no network buffer for a send or a connect, the call fails at once with `ENOBUFS`, even though the socket itself has room. Linux makes the sender wait instead, so the same program sees no error there. Sockets that hold much data nobody reads bring it on; some virtual machines, such as GitHub's macOS runners, also get it in short bursts with buffers far from any limit.

giong makes macOS behave like Linux for a while: a stream write or connect that gets `ENOBUFS` is tried again after 1 ms, then 2, 4, 8, 16 and every 32 ms (each step varied by up to a quarter), and fails with this code only when buffers have stayed short for 2 seconds. The worker runs its other tasks in the meantime. A `time::timeout` shorter than that ends the wait first, with its own error, and dropping the future cancels it with nothing sent. A connect whose socket could not be made for want of buffers (`socket(2)` fails with `ENOBUFS` too) makes it again, and one whose handshake the shortage broke is tried again on a new socket, within the same 2 seconds.

Calls that wait, then raise this code: `TcpStream` and `UnixStream` connects (including making their socket), writes and `send_file`, and giong-tls sends.

Calls that return the kernel's `ENOBUFS` as it is, with no code, as on Linux:

- datagram sends (`UdpSocket`), since a datagram may be dropped;
- accepts (`TcpListener::accept`, `UnixListener::accept`); try again after a short pause, as the giong-http server does;
- setup calls: the `bind` functions of `TcpListener`, `UdpSocket` and `UnixListener`, and `UnixStream::pair`.

## How to fix it

- Read from every connection promptly, and close the ones you no longer read from: each socket holds up to its receive buffer (`SO_RCVBUF`) of unread data.
- Cap the number of connections that can hold unread data at once (a semaphore around the work, or a lower connection limit on the server).
- Lower `SO_RCVBUF` and `SO_SNDBUF` if the program raised them.
- `netstat -m` shows how many requests for network buffers were denied. If the error comes with little in use, treat it as transient: try the operation again later, or on a new connection.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0060.md -->

# GIONG-E0060: a file is already at the Unix socket path

Raised by `UnixListener::bind` on Windows. In code: `giong::error::Code::UnixSocketInUse`. The error kind is `AddrInUse`, and Winsock's `WSAEADDRINUSE` is the `source()`.

## What happened

A Unix domain socket that listens is a file at its path. When the listener closes, the file stays, on Windows as on Unix, and a second bind to the same path fails while it is there. giong does not remove the file for you: another server may still be listening on it, and taking its path would leave that server unreachable.

## How to fix it

- If no server listens on the path any more (an earlier run of the same program, say), remove the file with `std::fs::remove_file` and bind again. A service usually does this at start-up, after making sure no other copy of itself runs.
- Otherwise pick another path, or stop the server that holds it.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0061.md -->

# GIONG-E0061: Unix socket path too long

Raised by `UnixListener::bind` and `UnixStream::connect` on Windows. In code: `giong::error::Code::UnixPathTooLong`. The error kind is `InvalidInput`.

## What happened

Winsock keeps the path of a Unix domain socket in a fixed field of 108 bytes, in UTF-8 and ending with a NUL, so a path may be at most 107 bytes long. Characters outside ASCII take two to four bytes each. The path is not shortened for you, since a shorter path names another socket.

## How to fix it

- Use a shorter path: a relative one (it is resolved against the current directory), or a directory near the root of the drive, such as `C:\run\app.sock`.
- `UnixStream::pair` binds a short-lived socket in the temporary directory (`std::env::temp_dir()`); if that directory's path is very long, point the `TMP` environment variable at a shorter one.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0062.md -->

# GIONG-E0062: no Unix domain sockets on this Windows

Raised by `UnixListener::bind`, `UnixStream::connect` and `UnixStream::pair` on Windows. In code: `giong::error::Code::UnixSocketsUnavailable`. The error kind is `Unsupported`, and Winsock's error (`WSAEAFNOSUPPORT` or similar) is in the message.

## What happened

Windows has had Unix domain stream sockets (`AF_UNIX`) since Windows 10 version 1803 and Windows Server 2019. On an older system, or one where the `afunix` driver is turned off, creating such a socket fails.

## How to fix it

- Run on Windows 10 version 1803 or later, or Windows Server 2019 or later, and check that `sc query afunix` shows the driver running.
- Otherwise talk over TCP on a loopback address (`127.0.0.1`) instead.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0090.md -->

# GIONG-E0090: IPC message too large

Raised by `giong::ipc::Sender::send`. In code: `giong::error::Code::IpcMessageTooLarge`.

## What happened

The message is longer than the channel carries. A message may take at most a quarter of the channel's capacity (the capacity of one direction, chosen by `giong::ipc::connect`), less 8 bytes for its record head, so that it always fits in the ring even when it has to start again at the beginning. `Sender::max_message` says the limit. Nothing was sent.

## How to fix it

- Connect with a larger capacity: a channel of `1 << 22` bytes (4 MiB per direction) takes messages up to 1 MiB minus 8 bytes. The listener must allow it (`IpcListener::bind`'s limit).
- Or split large payloads into several messages, or send them another way (a file, a pipe) and send a short message that names them.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0091.md -->

# GIONG-E0091: IPC channel memory corrupted

Raised by `giong::ipc::Sender::send` and `giong::ipc::Receiver::recv`. In code: `giong::error::Code::IpcCorrupted`.

## What happened

The other process wrote something into the channel's shared memory that breaks its rules: a read or write position out of range, or a message length that points past the data written. giong checks every position and length it reads from shared memory, so it stopped instead of reading or writing outside the channel. The message says which value was wrong. The channel cannot be trusted any more.

Causes: the other process writes into the mapping by its own means, runs a giong version with another channel layout under the same protocol version (a bug), or is hostile.

## How to fix it

- Drop both halves and connect again.
- Check that the other process uses `giong::ipc` of the same giong version and does not touch the shared memory itself.
- If both sides are unchanged giong code, report it with both versions: it is a bug.

[All error codes](https://giong.run/docs/errors.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.5.1/docs/errors/E0092.md -->

# GIONG-E0092: IPC capacity out of range

Raised by `giong::ipc::connect`, `giong::ipc::IpcListener::bind` and `IpcListener::accept`. In code: `giong::error::Code::IpcCapacity`.

## What happened

An IPC channel's capacity (the bytes of one direction's ring) must be a power of two from 4096 to 2^30 (1 GiB), and at most the limit the listener was bound with. Either the number given is not such a power of two, or the connecting process asked for more than the listener allows; the listener then refuses the channel and keeps listening.
